blocks.h: 1. What big data means in a maritime setting

blocks.p: Big data describes datasets whose volume, velocity and variety exceed what conventional tools can store, process and analyse; veracity and value are usually added, because data that is unreliable or that supports no decision is a cost rather than an asset. In the maritime sector the point is not that the industry has recently begun generating data - ships have kept logs for centuries - but that a modern ship is in effect a distributed sensor network, continuously producing machinery, navigation, cargo and environmental data which can now be transmitted, pooled across a fleet and analysed ashore.

It is also worth classifying what arrives, because it dictates what can be done with it: structured data already fits a defined field - noon-report figures, sensor readings, cargo manifests; unstructured data does not - photographs of corrosion, inspection narratives, voice and video; and semi-structured data carries its own tags without a fixed schema, which is what most machinery and messaging feeds actually look like. The distinction that matters is between data and information. Big data is only useful where analytics turn it into something a person can act on; volume without interpretation simply moves the problem.

One point of regulatory hard edge belongs at the start, because at this sitting digital data exchange is no longer voluntary. The 2022 amendments to the annex of the FAL Convention, resolution FAL.14(46) adopted on 13 May 2022, entered into force on 1 January 2024 under the tacit acceptance procedure. Standard 1.3quin now requires public authorities to introduce arrangements to enable the provision of all the information required under Standard 2.1 to a "single window" by electronic means, and to consider that single window as the channel through which they communicate decisions. The Convention defines a single window as "an environment that allows for the submission or provision of standardized and harmonized information and declarations to a single entry point, typically by electronic means". In the FAL Convention a Standard is mandatory, a Recommended Practice is not - so this is an obligation, and it took effect two months before this examination.

ul: Machinery. Engine power, revolutions, fuel rack or index position, exhaust and scavenge temperatures and pressures, turbocharger speeds, torque and shaft power meters.
Condition monitoring. Vibration analysis, lubricating oil and scrape-down analysis, thermography, and the continuous record held by the alarm and monitoring system.
Navigation. AIS, ECDIS, GNSS, gyro, echo sounder, radar and the voyage data recorder.
Hull and voyage. Speed through water and over ground, draught and trim, rudder angle, weather routeing and metocean feeds, and hull and propeller condition.
Cargo. Reefer container monitoring, tank gauging, loading computer output, temperature and humidity, and increasingly IoT tags at package level.
Fuel and emissions. Mass flow meters and tank soundings, feeding the mandatory fuel oil consumption reporting regimes.

Shore side. Port call and terminal operating systems, customs and single-window declarations, classification society records, port State control databases, satellite imagery and AIS aggregation services.

blocks.p: The weakest element is the one the industry has relied on longest: the manually compiled noon report, which is low frequency, self-reported and inconsistent. Much of the value of automated acquisition lies simply in replacing it.

ul: Voyage optimisation. Weather routeing against measured ship response rather than assumed performance, and just-in-time arrival - slowing to a berth-ready time instead of steaming hard and waiting at anchor, which saves fuel that no engine modification can.
Trim and speed optimisation. Measured resistance across draught and trim combinations, so the ship is operated at the point the data shows rather than the point the trim table assumes.

Hull and propeller performance. Continuous monitoring separates the fouling penalty from weather and loading effects, which allows hull cleaning and propeller polishing to be timed on evidence and the payback of a coating or an energy-saving device to be measured rather than asserted.

Condition-based maintenance. The largest single change to the Chief Engineer's work. Vibration signatures, lube oil particle counts and temperature trends give warning of bearing, liner and turbocharger deterioration, so overhauls move from a calendar interval to a demonstrated need - reducing both unnecessary opening-up and unexpected failure.
Fuel management. Consumption verification against bunker delivery notes, bunker quality trending, and detection of loss or discrepancy.
Commercial performance. Charterparty speed and consumption warranties are now argued from continuously logged data rather than from noon reports.

blocks.p: This has acquired regulatory consequence. Ship energy efficiency is now assessed not only by design but by operational outcome, and an operational rating is computed from exactly the consumption and distance data described above. Data quality has therefore stopped being purely a commercial matter.

blocks.h: 4. Port management, cargo tracking and safety

ul: Port management. Berth allocation, ETA prediction, pilot and tug scheduling, yard and gate planning, and port call optimisation. The Maritime Single Window is the regulatory spine of this: mandatory from 1 January 2024, it replaces repeated submission of the same information to different authorities. The Convention's design principle is submit once and re-use to the maximum extent possible, and Standard 2.1bis caps what may be demanded - public authorities shall not require more than the information shown in appendix 1.

Cargo tracking. Container-level visibility across the chain, reefer and cold-chain integrity monitoring with alarm before spoilage rather than a claim after it, and control of demurrage and detention exposure.

Maritime safety. The shift is from investigating casualties one at a time to analysing them in aggregate. Casualty and near-miss databases expose recurring causal patterns; port State control deficiency data drives the risk-based targeting used by the regional memoranda; AIS traffic density analysis informs routeing measures, traffic separation and VTS design; hours-of-rest and fatigue analytics identify manning pressure; and machinery analytics turn alarms from reactive into predictive.

blocks.p: The essential change is from reactive to anticipatory decision-making: acting on a trend rather than on a failure. It operates at three levels, and a good answer separates them.

ul: Shipboard, immediate. A rising bearing temperature trend, a change in vibration signature, a fuel consumption step change - decisions in hours.
Shore technical and fleet, medium term. Maintenance planning, spares provisioning, dry-docking scope, hull cleaning intervals - decisions in weeks and months.
Commercial and strategic, long term. Retrofit business cases, fleet renewal, trade selection and compliance planning - decisions in years.

blocks.p: Two further effects are worth stating. Fleet benchmarking exposes the outlier ship that her own crew cannot see, because they have no comparator. And regulatory reporting has become a decision input rather than only an output - an operational efficiency rating affects how a ship can be traded, so the data feeds the commercial decision instead of merely recording it.

For a Chief Engineer the relationship is a specific one. You are simultaneously the largest producer of this data and the person best placed to interpret it. The analytics reports a trend; the engineer decides what it means and what to do. Preserving that division - and the competence that underpins it - is itself a management responsibility.

ul: Connectivity. Bandwidth at sea has improved greatly but remains variable and costly compared with shore, so systems must be designed to filter and aggregate on board and to tolerate long periods offline.

Data quality - the dominant problem. Uncalibrated or drifting sensors, manual entry, and inconsistent measurement bases, such as speed through water against speed over ground or fuel by mass against by volume. Analytics does not improve bad data; it launders it into confident-looking output, which is more dangerous than no output at all.

Standardisation and interoperability. There is no universally adopted ship data model. Equipment from many makers uses proprietary formats and closed interfaces, so integration is a bespoke project on each ship.
Legacy tonnage. Older ships were never instrumented for this. Retrofitting flow meters, torque meters and networked sensors costs real money on an asset that may have few years remaining.

IT and OT convergence. Extracting data from operational technology - the systems that actually control machinery - is technically harder and riskier than extracting it from administrative systems, and it is where the security problem begins.

Cyber risk. The direct consequence of the previous point. Connecting operational technology to shore multiplies the attack surface, and a compromise reaches propulsion, steering or cargo systems rather than merely an office network. At this sitting the governing guidance is MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3/Rev.3, and resolution MSC.428(98) requires cyber risks to be addressed in the safety management system - so this is an ISM obligation, not an IT preference.

Data ownership and confidentiality. Owner, charterer, manager and equipment maker all claim rights in the same data stream, and contracts frequently do not say who owns it. Owners are reasonably wary that performance data will be used adversarially in a charterparty dispute.
Split incentives. On a time charter the owner buys the sensor and the charterer saves the fuel. Until the contract allocates the benefit, the investment case is weak for whoever must pay.
Industry structure. Shipping is fragmented into very many small owners, which slows the emergence of any common standard and prevents the scale that makes analytics cheap.
Cost and uncertain return. Benefits are real but hull-specific and hard to attribute, particularly on older tonnage with limited remaining life.

Skills and culture. Seagoing and superintendent staff need enough analytics literacy to challenge an output. Training and recruitment lag the technology, and a system nobody trusts is a system nobody uses.
Crew privacy. Where monitoring extends from machinery to people - hours worked, location, behaviour - there are legitimate data protection and industrial relations limits.

Regulatory fragmentation. Different reporting regimes demand differently shaped data for the same voyage, and port systems differ between and within States, which is precisely the problem the Single Window obligation is intended to reduce.

Automation bias. The subtlest barrier is one of judgement: decision support becoming, in practice, an unexamined decision maker. A model trained on normal operation is least reliable in exactly the abnormal conditions where a good decision matters most.

blocks.p: The marks are 8 + 8 and limb (A) names five segments - shipping operations, port management, fleet optimisation, cargo tracking and maritime safety. It is a coverage test, and route steps 3 and 4 exist so that all five are reached. Limb (B) has two distinct halves: role in decision-making, then evaluate the challenges and barriers. "Evaluate" is the higher command word on the paper, so steps 6 and 7 carry the greater weight.

The single thing that lifts this answer above a general essay is route step 1's dated instrument. Any candidate can write about analytics; very few can say that the Maritime Single Window became mandatory on 1 January 2024 under FAL Standard 1.3quin, two months before the paper. One sentence, and it changes the register of the whole answer.

blocks.h: The one hard instrument, and how to use it

blocks.p: Resolution FAL.14(46), adopted 13 May 2022, amended the annex to the FAL Convention and entered into force on 1 January 2024 by tacit acceptance. Standard 1.3quin obliges public authorities to enable all Standard 2.1 information to be provided to a single window by electronic means. Two supporting points are cheap to remember and show real reading: in the FAL Convention a Standard is mandatory while a Recommended Practice is not; and Standard 2.1bis caps the demand - authorities shall not require more than the information in appendix 1.

ul: Writing a general artificial-intelligence essay. The examiner asked about the maritime sector and named five segments.
Quoting percentage savings. They are vendor figures, hull-specific, and an examiner who knows the field will discount the whole answer.
Missing the regulatory anchor entirely and losing the one dated, citable fact available.
Treating limb (B) as a list of benefits. It asks you to evaluate challenges and barriers.
Ignoring data quality, which is the barrier practitioners rate first and candidates mention last.
Forgetting the cyber consequence of connecting operational technology to shore.
Data is not information. Say so early; it frames everything after it.
The noon report. Naming it as the weak link shows operational understanding rather than brochure knowledge.
Split incentives. The owner-buys / charterer-saves problem is the commercial reason adoption is slower than the technology allows, and almost nobody writes it.
Speed through water against speed over ground. A concrete, checkable example of inconsistent measurement basis.
Automation bias. A model is least reliable in the abnormal conditions where the decision matters most. This is the mature closing point.
"What is the Maritime Single Window and when did it become mandatory?" - FAL Standard 1.3quin, from 1 January 2024, under the FAL.14(46) amendments.

"Give a practical example of condition-based maintenance in your engine room." - vibration and lube oil trending on a turbocharger or main bearing, with the overhaul triggered by trend rather than running hours.
"How would you know your hull needed cleaning?" - performance monitoring separating the fouling penalty from weather and loading, not a fixed interval.
"What is the risk in connecting the engine control system to a shore network?" - it is an operational technology exposure; MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3/Rev.3 and MSC.428(98) make it an ISM matter.
"Whose data is it?" - contested between owner, charterer, manager and maker; usually a contractual gap.

blocks.p: Limb (A) is SOURCE - SHIP - SHORE: where the data comes from (2), what it does at sea (3), what it does in port and for safety (4). Limb (B) is DECIDE - THEN WHAT STOPS IT: decision levels (5), then barriers split into technical (6) and human and commercial (7).
For the barriers, five words in order of practitioner priority: QUALITY, CONNECTIVITY, STANDARDS, SECURITY, OWNERSHIP.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the limits of this answer

blocks.p: This question sits substantially outside the regulatory corpus, and the answer is written to say so rather than to disguise it. The FAL material is primary and was read. Everything else - data sources, analytics applications, decision levels and barriers - is engineering and industry practice, presented as reasoning rather than as citation.

No percentage figures appear anywhere. Published claims for fuel saving or emissions benefit from analytics vary by an order of magnitude, are specific to hull and trade, and none was verifiable from a primary source. A mechanism explained is worth more in an examination than a number that cannot be defended.

The efficiency-rating framing in route step 3 is deliberately expressed without regulation numbers. The MARPOL Annex VI provisions were not read in a licensed consolidated edition for this question, so the answer states the effect and not a citation.

questions.understand_first:
Big data is not simply a lot of data. What makes it a different kind of problem is that it arrives faster than anyone can look at it, in forms that will not sit in neat rows and columns, from sources of very uneven trustworthiness - and it is worth nothing at all until something turns it into a decision. That last clause is the whole subject. A sensor logging a bearing temperature every second has produced data; a system that notices the trend and has the bearing renewed before it fails has produced value. The formal way of saying this is the five Vs - volume, velocity, variety, veracity and value - but the ideas underneath them are ordinary: too much, too fast, too mixed, not all of it true, and pointless unless someone acts on it.

In shipping the raw material already exists and mostly goes unused - machinery telemetry, position reports, fuel and cargo figures, port records. Each segment named in the question is the same move applied to a different decision: what speed to run, when to open a machine up, when a berth will be free, where a container actually is, and which risks are building before they become casualties. The honest half of the answer is the barriers, and they are not computing power. They are whether the data can be trusted, how it gets ashore, who owns it, who pays for the sensor when somebody else banks the saving, and the exposure created by connecting machinery to the shore at all.

retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What big data means at sea, and the FAL single window obligation. 2 (A) Where the data comes from. 3 (A) Shipping operations and fleet optimisation. 4 (A) Port management, cargo tracking and safety. 5 (B) How decision-making changes. 6 (B) Technical and data barriers. 7 (B) Commercial, human and regulatory barriers.
retrieval_cards.why: Steps 3 and 4 exist to cover the five segments the examiner named.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the Maritime Single Window obligation, and when did it take effect?
retrieval_cards.answer: FAL Convention annex Standard 1.3quin, as amended by resolution FAL.14(46) adopted 13 May 2022, in force 1 January 2024. Public authorities shall introduce arrangements to enable all information required under Standard 2.1 to be provided to a single window by electronic means. A "Standard" in the FAL Convention is mandatory.
retrieval_cards.why: The only dated, mandatory, citable instrument on this question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the FAL Convention define a single window?
retrieval_cards.answer: An environment that allows for the submission or provision of standardized and harmonized information and declarations to a single entry point, typically by electronic means. The design principle is submit once and re-use to the maximum extent possible.
retrieval_cards.why: Quoting the definition is worth more than describing the concept.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the first barrier to maritime big data, and why is it worse than no data?
retrieval_cards.answer: Data quality. Uncalibrated or drifting sensors, manual noon-report entry and inconsistent measurement bases such as speed through water against speed over ground. Analytics does not improve bad data; it turns it into confident-looking output, which is more dangerous than no output because it is acted upon.
retrieval_cards.why: Practitioners rate this first; candidates mention it last, if at all.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Explain the split-incentive problem in maritime data investment.
retrieval_cards.answer: On a time charter the owner pays for the sensors, the monitoring system and the bandwidth, while the charterer pays for and therefore saves the fuel. Unless the charterparty allocates the benefit, neither party has a complete business case, which slows adoption independently of the technology.
retrieval_cards.why: The commercial reason adoption lags the technology, and rarely written.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the three decision levels big data supports, with a timescale for each.
retrieval_cards.answer: Shipboard and immediate - a temperature or vibration trend, decided in hours. Shore technical and fleet, medium term - maintenance planning, spares, dry-dock scope, hull cleaning, decided in weeks to months. Commercial and strategic, long term - retrofit business cases, fleet renewal and trade selection, decided in years.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (B) asks about decision-making; separating the levels is what "discuss" means.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the cyber consequence of maritime big data, and which instruments apply?
retrieval_cards.answer: Connecting operational technology to shore multiplies the attack surface, and a compromise can reach propulsion, steering or cargo systems rather than only an office network. At this sitting the guidance is MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3/Rev.3, and resolution MSC.428(98) requires cyber risks to be addressed in the safety management system - making it an ISM obligation.
retrieval_cards.why: Links this question to Q5 of the same paper and shows the regime, not just the risk.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why should you give no percentage savings figures in this answer?
retrieval_cards.answer: Published figures for fuel or emissions benefit from analytics vary by an order of magnitude, are specific to hull, trade and baseline, and originate largely from vendors. An unverifiable number invites challenge and devalues the surrounding answer; an explained mechanism does not.
retrieval_cards.why: The most common way a good big-data answer loses credibility.

blocks.h: 1. What a bill of lading is, and the law that governs it

blocks.p: A bill of lading is a document issued by or on behalf of the carrier to the shipper on receipt or shipment of goods. Neither Indian nor English law defines it by a single formula; it is defined by what it does, and the Indian Sale of Goods Act, 1930, section 2(4) reflects this by including a bill of lading within the expression "document of title to goods".

At this sitting the Indian statute book is new. The governing framework is the Bills of Lading Act, 2025 (Act 18 of 2025), which deals with the transfer of rights and liabilities under the bill, and the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025 (Act 19 of 2025), whose Schedule carries the carriage regime. Both came into force on 10 September 2025 - about five weeks before this examination - repealing the Indian Bills of Lading Act, 1856 (s.6(1) of the 2025 Act) and the Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 (s.12(1)) respectively.

The Act gives force of law to the Hague Rules as amended by the Protocols of 1968 and 1979 - the Hague-Visby regime - but expressly "as so amended and as set out with modifications in the Schedule". The Indian Schedule, not the international text, is the law here. Schedule Article I(c) is the gateway: the rules apply only to contracts of carriage covered by a bill of lading or any similar document of title. The Hamburg Rules 1978 are in force internationally but India is not a party; the Rotterdam Rules 2008 are not in force. Both are worth naming for completeness and must not be applied.

blocks.h: 2. The three functions, and their commercial significance

ul: A receipt for the goods. Article III(3) requires the carrier, master or agent, on the shipper's demand, to issue a bill showing (a) the leading marks necessary for identification, (b) either the number of packages or pieces, or the quantity, or weight, and (c) the apparent order and condition of the goods. The proviso matters in practice: no carrier is bound to state marks, number, quantity or weight which he has reasonable ground for suspecting not accurately to represent the goods, or which he has had no reasonable means of checking - the basis of the "said to contain" and "shipper's weight and count" reservations.

Evidence of the contract of carriage. The bill is not the contract itself - the contract is normally concluded when the space is booked, before any bill exists. Between carrier and shipper the bill is evidence of the terms; once it passes to a third-party holder its terms become the contract as between carrier and holder.

A document of title. Possession of the bill gives constructive possession of the goods, and an order bill is transferable by endorsement and delivery. This is the function that carries the commerce: it lets goods be sold and resold while at sea, lets a seller on CIF or FOB terms be paid against documents, and lets a bank take the bill as security under a documentary credit.

blocks.p: The evidential force strengthens on transfer. Article III(4) makes the bill prima facie evidence of receipt of the goods as described, but proof to the contrary is not admissible once the bill has been transferred to a third party acting in good faith - the Visby addition, carried into the 2025 Schedule, and the reason a buyer or bank can rely on the document.

One Indian enacting provision belongs here because it is unique to the statute and easy marks: section 5 requires that every bill of lading issued in India contain an express statement that it has effect subject to the applicable rules. That is the statutory clause paramount, and it means the regime cannot be quietly contracted out of at the document-drafting stage.

blocks.h: 3. The bill issued to the ship, and its counterpart

blocks.p: A bill issued to the ship is one issued by the master, or by an agent signing "for the Master" on the shipowner's behalf - commonly called an owner's bill. Under it the shipowner is the contracting carrier and bears the Article III obligations personally.

Its counterpart is the charterer's bill, signed by or for the charterer, under which the charterer is the carrier and the shipowner is not a party to the contract of carriage at all. The Schedule expressly contemplates both: Article I(b) provides that "carrier" includes the owner or the charterer who enters into a contract of carriage with a shipper, and Article I(c) brings a bill issued under or pursuant to a charterparty within the rules from the moment at which it regulates the relations between a carrier and a holder - that is, once it is endorsed away from the charterer. Article V completes the picture: the rules do not apply to charterparties as such, but bills issued under one must comply.

The distinction is not academic. It determines whom the cargo claimant sues, whether the claim lies in contract or only in bailment or tort, and whose P&I cover responds. In practice it is resolved by reading the signature box, any identity of carrier clause and any demise clause. A third document must be kept separate: the house bill issued by a freight forwarder or NVOCC, which is not issued by or for the ship at all and under which the forwarder contracts as carrier.

blocks.h: 4. The other principal types and their purposes

ul: Shipped (on board) against received for shipment. Only the first states that the goods have actually been loaded. Documentary credits normally require an on-board bill, and a received-for-shipment bill is converted by an on-board notation. Article III(7) gives the shipper the right to demand a shipped bill.

Clean against claused or foul. A clean bill carries no clause expressly declaring a defective condition of goods or packaging, under Article III(3)(c). A claused bill is normally rejected under a letter of credit, which is exactly why shippers press for a clean bill against a letter of indemnity - a practice which is improper where the clausing would have been accurate, because it deceives the third-party holder.

Order, bearer and straight bills. An order bill ("to order" or "to order of X") is negotiable by endorsement; a bearer bill passes by delivery; a straight bill names a consignee and is not negotiable, so it cannot be used to resell the goods in transit.
Through and combined transport (multimodal) bills, covering carriage by more than one carrier or by more than one mode, with the issuer taking responsibility across the legs.

Sea waybill. A receipt and evidence of the contract, but NOT a document of title. It is non-negotiable, delivery is made to the named consignee on proof of identity, and no original need be presented - which is why it suits trades with no resale in transit and short voyages where the cargo outruns the paperwork.

Switch bills - a second set issued in place of the first, usually to conceal the true load port or shipper. Legitimate uses exist but the fraud risk is high and the first set must be surrendered. Stale bills are those tendered too late to be taken up under the credit.

blocks.h: 5. The carrier's obligations under the Rules

blocks.p: Under the 2025 Schedule the carrier - whether shipowner or charterer - carries two positive duties and one duty to document.

ul: Article III(1) - seaworthiness. The carrier is bound before and at the beginning of the voyage to exercise due diligence to (a) make the ship seaworthy; (b) properly man, equip and supply the ship; and (c) make the holds, refrigerating and cool chambers, and all other parts of the ship in which goods are carried, fit and safe for their reception, carriage and preservation. Two qualifications earn marks: it is a duty of due diligence, not an absolute warranty - and section 4 of the Act says so expressly, providing that there is no implied absolute undertaking of seaworthiness - and it attaches before and at the beginning of the voyage, so it is not a continuing obligation once the voyage has begun.

Article III(2) - care of cargo. Subject to Article IV, the carrier shall properly and carefully load, handle, stow, carry, keep, care for and discharge the goods. Seven verbs, and they are worth reproducing exactly.
Article III(3) and (7) - documentation. Issue the bill on demand, showing the three matters at §2 above, and a shipped bill on demand once the goods are loaded.

blocks.p: Two boundaries define the reach of those duties, and one of them is where Indian law now departs from the international text. Article I(a) - "carriage of goods" covers only the period from the time when the goods are loaded on to the time they are discharged, the tackle to tackle rule; that is unchanged.

Article I(d) is where the Indian text departs, and it runs in the cargo owner's favour. "Goods" INCLUDES any property, including live animals, as well as containers, pallets or similar articles of transport or packaging supplied by the consignor, irrespective of whether such property is to be or is carried on or under deck. Live animals and deck cargo are therefore inside the compulsory regime in India, and the carrier cannot take a cargo outside it by stating deck carriage on the face of the bill.

Against contracting out, Article III(8) is absolute: any clause relieving the carrier or the ship from liability for negligence, fault or failure in these duties, or lessening such liability otherwise than as provided in these rules, shall be null and void and of no effect - and by Article III(9) a benefit-of-insurance clause is deemed to be such a clause. Contracting to increase the carrier's liability remains permitted.

blocks.h: 6. Immunities, the package limitation and the time bar

blocks.p: Against those duties the Schedule gives the carrier a defined set of protections. The balance between the two is the whole of the Hague-Visby compromise, and it survives in Indian law with the modifications noted.

ul: Article IV(1). No liability for loss from unseaworthiness unless caused by want of due diligence - and the burden of proving due diligence is on the carrier.

Article IV(2) - the excepted perils, seventeen in all. Two matter most: (a) act, neglect or default of the master, mariner, pilot or the servants of the carrier in the navigation or in the management of the ship - the nautical fault defence, abolished by the Hamburg Rules and retained here - and (b) fire, unless caused by the actual fault or privity of the carrier. The rest run through perils of the sea, act of God, war, public enemies, arrest or restraint, quarantine, act or omission of the shipper, strikes, riots, saving life or property, inherent vice and wastage, insufficiency of packing or marks, latent defects not discoverable by due diligence, and the catch-all at (q), on which the carrier bears the burden.
Article IV(4) - deviation. Deviation in saving or attempting to save life or property at sea, and any reasonable deviation, is not a breach.

Article IV(5)(a) - package limitation. Unless the nature and value were declared by the shipper before shipment and inserted in the bill, liability is capped at 666.67 units of account per package or unit or 2 units of account per kilogramme of gross weight, whichever is the higher. The unit of account is the Special Drawing Right. Article IV(5)(b) is the container clause: where goods are consolidated, the number of packages enumerated in the bill is the number of packages, and otherwise the container itself is one package.

Article IV(5)(c) - loss of the limit, where the damage resulted from an act or omission done with intent to cause damage, or recklessly and with knowledge that damage would probably result. Note the lettering: this is (c) in the Indian Schedule, not the Hague-Visby (e).
Article IV(6) - dangerous goods, which the carrier may land, destroy or render innocuous, with the shipper liable for the consequences.

Article III(6) - the time bar, AND the Indian addition. Carrier and ship are discharged from all liability whatsoever unless suit is brought within ONE YEAR of delivery or of when the goods should have been delivered, extendable by agreement made after the cause of action has arisen. The Indian Schedule then adds a proviso the international text does not contain: a suit may be brought after that year within a further period of not more than THREE MONTHS as allowed by the court. That is a judicial extension, not a contractual one, and it is a real difference in the claimant's favour.

blocks.p: The Schedule runs Articles I to IX and contains no Article IV bis. There is therefore no statutory extension of the defences and limits to claims framed in tort, or to the carrier's servants and agents: protection for stevedores and sub-contractors depends on the Himalaya clause in the contract itself.

blocks.h: 7. Shipowner, consignee, and the transfer of rights

blocks.p: Where the bill is an owner's bill the shipowner is the carrier and every duty in §5 is his. Where it is a charterer's bill he is not a party to the contract of carriage, but he is not immune: he holds the goods as bailee, and the Schedule consistently says "neither the carrier nor the ship" - the vessel herself is exposed, including to arrest in rem. The shipper also owes a duty: under Article III(5) he guarantees the accuracy of the marks, number, quantity and weight he furnishes and indemnifies the carrier against inaccuracy.

The consignee is brought into the contract by the Bills of Lading Act, 2025. Its three operative sections re-enact the scheme of the 1856 Act rather than reforming it, so the substance a candidate learned before September 2025 still holds - only the citation has moved:

ul: Section 2 - every consignee named in the bill, and every endorsee to whom property passes upon or by reason of the consignment or endorsement, has all rights of suit transferred to and vested in him and is subject to the same liabilities as if the contract had been made with himself. Rights and burdens move together. (1856 Act s.1.)
Section 3 - the right of stoppage in transit and the shipowner's claim for freight against the original shipper or owner are preserved. (1856 Act s.2.)

Section 4(1) - the bill in the hands of a consignee or endorsee for valuable consideration is conclusive evidence of shipment as against the master or other person signing, even if the goods were never shipped - subject to a fraud proviso. It bites on the master personally. (1856 Act s.3.) Section 4(2) adds that it does not so operate where the holder had actual notice that the goods were not in fact laden.

blocks.p: Two Indian enacting provisions round off limb (c). Section 3 of the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 2025 fixes the geographical reach: the applicable rules have effect for carriage from any port in India to any other port, whether in or outside India - outward voyages, so an inward shipment is governed by the rules only if the contract so provides. And section 12(3) preserves section 331 and Part XA of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, so the shipowner's general limitation of liability sits alongside, and is not displaced by, the package limitation.

In performance the consignee must present an original bill to take delivery, pay freight where payable and give security for any general average contribution. The mirror obligation is the one most often broken: delivery without production of an original bill is at the carrier's own peril, and a letter of indemnity does not change that as against the true holder - it merely gives the carrier someone to sue.

The marks are 3 + 5 + 8 and the weighting is unusually explicit. Limb (a) is worth three marks - a definition and the three functions, and no more; candidates routinely spend a page on it. Limb (b) at five marks wants distinctions with purposes, which is why route step 4 gives each type a purpose in one line rather than a paragraph. Limb (c) carries half the question and asks for three parties and cited law, which is why route steps 5, 6 and 7 are the longest.

The single highest-value habit on limb (c) is to cite the Article and clause number. "The carrier must exercise due diligence to make the ship seaworthy before and at the beginning of the voyage" is a good sentence; "Article III(1)" in front of it is a mark.

blocks.h: THE TEMPORAL POINT - the Indian statute book changed five weeks before this paper

blocks.p: This is the most important currentness note in the paper, and it is the reason this question cannot be answered from an older model answer. At this sitting the governing Acts are the Bills of Lading Act, 2025 (18 of 2025) and the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025 (19 of 2025), both in force from 10 September 2025. They repealed the Indian Bills of Lading Act, 1856 and the Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 respectively. A candidate citing the 1856 and 1925 Acts as current law at October 2025 is citing repealed statutes.

The two Acts behave very differently, and it is worth knowing which is which. The Bills of Lading Act 2025 re-enacts: its sections 2, 3 and 4 carry the same three subjects as sections 1, 2 and 3 of the 1856 Act, so everything you already knew about the transfer of rights is still right and only the section numbers moved. The Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 2025 does not: it gives the Hague-Visby regime force of law "with modifications", and four of those modifications matter.

blocks.h: The four modifications in the 2025 Schedule

ul: 1. "Goods" now INCLUDES live animals and deck cargo - Article I(d). Hague-Visby Article I(c) excluded both. The Indian Schedule reverses this and adds the words "irrespective of whether such property is to be or is carried on or under deck". Deck cargo can no longer be taken outside the regime by a statement on the bill. If you learned the old exclusion, unlearn it for Indian carriage.

2. Article IV bis is absent. The Schedule runs Articles I to IX and contains no "bis". The tort-channelling and servants-and-agents extension is simply not in the Indian text. Himalaya protection must come from the contract clause, not from the statute.

3. A three-month judicial extension of the one-year time bar - Article III(6)(c) proviso. Under Hague-Visby the year can be extended only by agreement after the cause of action arose. In India a court may allow a further period of not more than three months. The one-year rule is still the rule; the escape valve is new.

4. Article I and Article IV(5) are re-lettered. Carrier is now I(b), contract of carriage I(c), goods I(d), ship I(e), carriage of goods I(a); and loss of the limit is IV(5)(c), not IV(5)(e). Quoting the international lettering in an Indian answer is a small but avoidable error.

blocks.p: The substance of the carrier's duties and immunities is otherwise unchanged - Article III(1) and (2), the seventeen exceptions, 666.67 / 2 whichever higher, the one-year bar, Article III(8). This is why the route below is the same route that served the March 2024 sitting.

blocks.h: What "issued to the ship" means, and why the answer says so explicitly

blocks.p: The printed phrase is not a term of art, and part of the examiner's test is whether the candidate recognises what is being contrasted. Limb (c) asks for the obligations of the shipowner, the carrier and the consignee - naming shipowner and carrier separately. That is only meaningful if the two can be different people, which is exactly the owner's bill against charterer's bill distinction. The answer therefore reads "issued to the ship" as the owner's bill - issued by the master or "for the Master" - and says so in terms rather than assuming it.

If in the exam you are unsure, state your reading in one line and answer it. An examiner cannot penalise a clearly stated and reasonable construction; an examiner can penalise an answer that silently answers a different question.

ul: Citing the 1856 and 1925 Acts as current. Both were repealed with effect from 10 September 2025. Cite the 2025 Acts.
Saying "goods exclude live animals and deck cargo". True of Hague-Visby, and true of Indian law before 10 September 2025. False now - Article I(d) includes both.
Citing Article IV bis as Indian law. It is not in the Schedule.
Writing "a bill of lading is the contract of carriage". It is evidence of it. The contract predates the document.
Applying the Hamburg Rules to an Indian carriage. India is not a party. Name them, and the Rotterdam Rules, for status only.
Saying the seaworthiness obligation is absolute. It is due diligence, section 4 says so expressly, and it is not continuing.
Giving the package limitation as one figure. It is 666.67 SDR per package or unit OR 2 SDR per kilogramme, whichever is HIGHER.
Forgetting the one-year time bar, or quoting it without the Indian three-month judicial extension.
Treating a sea waybill as a bill of lading. It is not a document of title.
Answering limb (c) about the carrier only. Three parties were named.

Deck cargo no longer needs the two-limb test in India. Under Hague-Visby you asked whether the cargo was both stated as deck cargo and so carried. Under Article I(d) the question does not arise - deck or under deck, it is "goods". Candidates who have memorised the old two-limb test will apply it confidently and be wrong.
Tackle to tackle survives. Article I(a) - the rules cover loading to discharge, not the port terminal periods either side. That boundary did not move.
Article III(8). Contracting out downward is void; contracting to increase the carrier's liability is not.
Article III(4). Prima facie against the shipper, conclusive against a good-faith third-party transferee. The change on transfer is the point.

Nautical fault. Article IV(2)(a) protects negligent navigation or management of the ship, not negligent care of the cargo. The line between "management of the ship" and "care of cargo" is the most litigated boundary in the regime.

Section 4(1) of the Bills of Lading Act 2025 bites on the master personally - a worthwhile point for a Chief Engineer to know about the person signing. Section 4(2) is the holder's-actual-notice escape.
Outward voyages. Section 3 applies the rules to carriage from an Indian port outwards. Inward carriage is caught only by contract.
"Name the three functions of a bill of lading." - receipt, evidence of the contract, document of title.
"Which Act governs carriage of goods by sea from India today?" - the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 2025, in force 10 September 2025, which repealed the 1925 Act.
"Is deck cargo covered by the rules?" - in India, yes. Article I(d) includes property carried on or under deck, and live animals.

"Cargo is damaged. How long has the receiver got to sue?" - one year under Article III(6), extendable by agreement after the cause of action arose, and the court may allow a further period of not more than three months.
"Your holds were not cleaned and the cargo is contaminated. Which rule?" - Article III(1)(c), and the carrier must prove due diligence under Article IV(1).
"The bosun floods a hold by leaving a valve open. Is that nautical fault?" - it depends whether the act is management of the ship or care of the cargo; Article IV(2)(a) covers the former only.

"A receiver has lost the bill and wants his cargo. What do you do?" - delivery without an original is at the carrier's peril; refer to the owner and the P&I club, and expect a club-form letter of indemnity, usually bank-countersigned.
"Who is the carrier under your bill?" - read the signature box and any identity-of-carrier or demise clause.

blocks.p: For limb (a), three words: RECEIPT, EVIDENCE, TITLE. For limb (c), work the Schedule as a see-saw: Article III is what the carrier must do, Article IV is what he escapes, and the two hinges between them are Article III(8) (cannot contract out downward) and Article III(6) (one year, plus three months if the court allows).
For the numbers: one year plus three months, 666.67, 2, higher. For the statutes: 18 and 19 of 2025, both live on 10 September 2025.

ul: Sch. Art I(a) carriage of goods, tackle to tackle. I(b) carrier includes owner or charterer. I(c) contract of carriage - the gateway. I(d) goods INCLUDE live animals and deck cargo. I(e) ship.

Sch. Art III(1) due diligence, seaworthy / man, equip, supply / holds fit. (2) load, handle, stow, carry, keep, care for, discharge. (3) the bill and its three particulars. (4) prima facie, conclusive on transfer in good faith. (5) shipper's guarantee and indemnity. (6) one year, plus three months by the court. (7) shipped bill on demand. (8)-(9) null and void.

Sch. Art IV(1) unseaworthiness and the burden. (2)(a) nautical fault, (b) fire. (4) deviation. (5)(a) 666.67 / 2, whichever higher. (5)(b) container enumeration. (5)(c) loss of the limit. (6) dangerous goods. Art V charterparties. No Article IV bis.

Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 2025 - s.3 outward voyages; s.4 no implied absolute undertaking of seaworthiness; s.5 statutory clause paramount; s.9 Central Government may amend the Schedule; s.12(1) repeals the 1925 Act, s.12(3) preserves MS Act 1958 s.331 and Part XA.

Bills of Lading Act 2025 - s.2 rights of suit and liabilities pass; s.3 stoppage in transit and freight preserved; s.4(1) conclusive evidence against the signer, s.4(2) actual-notice exception; s.6(1) repeals the 1856 Act.
Indian Sale of Goods Act 1930 s.2(4) - document of title.

Why the new definition of "goods" matters commercially. Deck carriage was the standard way of putting a cargo outside the compulsory regime, so that the carrier could contract on his own terms - which is why the phrase "stated as carried on deck and so carried" appears on so many bills. Article I(d) closes that route in India. Containers carried on deck, which is most container carriage, are now squarely inside the regime, and the carrier's exposure is correspondingly wider. Live animals are in the same position.

Why the absence of Article IV bis is not the end of Himalaya protection. Article IV bis gave the defences statutory reach into tort and down to servants and agents. Without it, the carrier's stevedores and sub-contractors rely on the Himalaya clause drafted into the bill. The practical consequence is that the clause has to be there and has to be well drafted; the statute will not supply the protection.

Why "management of the ship" is the most litigated phrase in the regime. Article IV(2)(a) protects negligence in the navigation or management of the ship, but not negligence in the care of the cargo under Article III(2). The same act can fall either side: closing a valve to trim the vessel is management of the ship; closing it to protect a particular parcel is care of cargo. Where the purpose is mixed, the courts look at the dominant object of the act.

Why the limitation is expressed two ways. The package basis protects the carrier against a single high-value crate; the weight basis protects the cargo owner in bulk and heavy-lift trades where one "package" could be enormous. Taking whichever is higher means the claimant always gets the more favourable of the two.

The time bar is a true extinction, not a limitation period. Article III(6) says the carrier and the ship are discharged from all liability whatsoever. The Indian three-month judicial extension softens it but does not change its nature: outside the year, and outside any extension, the liability is gone rather than merely unenforceable.

Letters of indemnity in practice. Two situations recur and both are commercially normal and legally exposed: an LOI for a clean bill where clausing would have been accurate (which deceives the third-party holder and is generally unenforceable), and an LOI for delivery without the original bill (enforceable between the parties, but leaving the carrier liable to the true holder). Club forms exist for the second, usually requiring a bank counter-signature; the first is not a club-supported form.

blocks.p: Both 2025 Acts were read in full in the official Gazette of India, including the entire Schedule to the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act. Every Article citation in limb (c) is taken from the Indian enacted text, not from the Hague-Visby Rules as an international instrument - which matters, because the two differ in the four respects set out above. The absence of Article IV bis was established by searching the full extracted Schedule text, which returns no occurrence of "bis".

The text of the repealed 1856 and 1925 Acts could not be retrieved; India Code publishes current law only and removed both on repeal. Their identity and citation come from the repealing sections of the 2025 Acts. This matters much less than it once did, because this answer states the law under the 2025 Acts and mentions the old ones only as history.

The unit of account under Article IV(5) is the Special Drawing Right, named directly in the Schedule. The conversion machinery was not read, and no rupee figure is given anywhere. No case law is asserted; in particular, the effect of the new Article I(d) on the deck-cargo jurisprudence had not been judicially tested at this sitting.

questions.understand_first: A bill of lading is three things at once, and almost every examinable point follows from which of the three is in play. As a RECEIPT it records what was shipped and in what apparent order and condition. As EVIDENCE OF THE CONTRACT it carries the carriage terms - but it is not the contract, which was made earlier. As a DOCUMENT OF TITLE it lets the goods be sold, financed and delivered against paper while the ship is still at sea, and that is why international trade works at all. Limb (c) then asks who owes what, and the answer is in two places: the Schedule to the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 2025 for the carriage obligations, and the Bills of Lading Act 2025 for how those rights and liabilities move to the consignee. THE DATE WARNING IS THE WHOLE OF THIS QUESTION: both Acts came into force on 10 September 2025, five weeks before this paper, replacing the 1856 and 1925 Acts. And the new Schedule is not simply Hague-Visby renumbered - it INCLUDES live animals and deck cargo in "goods", drops Article IV bis, and lets a court extend the one-year time bar by three months. Learn the Indian text, not the international one.
questions.memory_cue: Limb (a) is three words - RECEIPT, EVIDENCE, TITLE (2). Limb (c) is a see-saw: Article III is what the carrier MUST DO (5), Article IV is what he ESCAPES (6), and the transfer of rights to the consignee sits in the Bills of Lading Act 2025 (7). Two Acts, two numbers: 18 and 19 of 2025, both alive on 10 September 2025. The numbers to hold: one year plus three months, 666.67, two, higher (6).

quick_revision.critical_regulation: Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 2025, Schedule Article III(1) - the carrier shall be bound, before and at the beginning of the voyage, to exercise due diligence to make the ship seaworthy, properly man, equip and supply her, and make the holds and all other cargo spaces fit and safe for reception, carriage and preservation. quick_revision.major_trap: Answering on the OLD Indian statute book, or on international Hague-Visby instead of the Indian Schedule. Both traps are live at this sitting. The Bills of Lading Act 2025 and the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 2025 came into force on 10 September 2025 - five weeks before this paper - and the 1856 and 1925 Acts are repealed. Worse, the 2025 Schedule is NOT Hague-Visby renumbered: Article I(d) INCLUDES live animals and property carried on or under deck, so the familiar exclusion of deck cargo is REVERSED in India; Article IV bis is absent altogether; and Article III(6)(c) lets a court allow a further three months beyond the one-year bar. A candidate who writes the well-known Hague-Visby answer will state a confident falsehood about deck cargo and cite an Article that is not in Indian law.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the three functions of a bill of lading?
retrieval_cards.answer: A receipt for the goods, showing leading marks, number or quantity or weight, and apparent order and condition (Schedule Article III(3)); evidence of the contract of carriage - not the contract itself; and a document of title, transferable by endorsement and delivery, included in "document of title to goods" by section 2(4) of the Indian Sale of Goods Act 1930.
retrieval_cards.why: Three marks, three functions. Anything longer is wasted.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Indian statutes governed the bill of lading at this sitting, and when did they come into force?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Bills of Lading Act, 2025 (Act 18 of 2025) and the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025 (Act 19 of 2025). BOTH came into force on 10 September 2025, five weeks before this examination, repealing the Indian Bills of Lading Act 1856 and the Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925 respectively.
retrieval_cards.why: The statute book changed on 10 September 2025, five weeks before this paper. Citing the 1856 or 1925 Act here is citing repealed law.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Under Indian law at this sitting, are live animals and deck cargo within "goods"?
retrieval_cards.answer: YES. Schedule Article I(d) defines "goods" to INCLUDE any property including live animals, as well as containers, pallets or similar articles of transport or packaging supplied by the consignor, IRRESPECTIVE of whether such property is to be or is carried on or under deck. This REVERSES the Hague-Visby Article I(c) exclusion. A carrier can no longer put deck cargo outside the regime by stating deck carriage on the bill.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the single most dangerous carry-over from an older answer. The familiar two-limb deck-cargo test does not apply in India at this sitting.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Can you cite Article IV bis in an Indian carriage answer at this sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The Schedule to the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 2025 runs Articles I to IX and contains no Article IV bis. The tort-channelling rule and the extension of defences to servants and agents are not part of the enacted Indian text. Himalaya protection must be found in the Himalaya clause in the contract, not in the statute.
retrieval_cards.why: A confident citation to an Article that does not exist in the governing text is worse than omitting the point.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between an owner's bill and a charterer's bill?
retrieval_cards.answer: An owner's bill is issued by the master or by an agent signing "for the Master", so the shipowner is the contracting carrier. A charterer's bill is signed by or for the charterer, who is then the carrier, and the shipowner is not a party to the contract of carriage. Schedule Article I(b) - "carrier" includes the owner or the charterer who enters into a contract of carriage with a shipper. It decides whom the cargo claimant sues and whose P&I cover responds.
retrieval_cards.why: This is what "issued to the ship" is contrasting, and limb (c) names both parties.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the carrier's two positive duties under Schedule Article III.
retrieval_cards.answer: Article III(1) - before and at the beginning of the voyage, exercise due diligence to make the ship seaworthy, properly man, equip and supply her, and make the holds, refrigerating and cool chambers and all other cargo spaces fit and safe for reception, carriage and preservation. Article III(2) - properly and carefully load, handle, stow, carry, keep, care for and discharge the goods.
retrieval_cards.why: Due diligence, not absolute - section 4 of the Act says so expressly - and it is not a continuing obligation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the package limitation and the time bar under the Indian Schedule.
retrieval_cards.answer: Article IV(5)(a) - unless nature and value were declared by the shipper before shipment and inserted in the bill, liability is limited to 666.67 units of account per package or unit, or 2 units of account per kilogramme of gross weight, whichever is the higher. Article III(6) - carrier and ship are discharged from all liability unless suit is brought within one year, extendable by agreement made after the cause of action arose, AND the court may allow a further period of not more than three months.
retrieval_cards.why: The three-month judicial extension is an Indian addition that the international text does not contain.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the Bills of Lading Act 2025 move rights to the consignee?
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 2 - the consignee named in the bill, and every endorsee to whom property passes by reason of the consignment or endorsement, has all rights of suit vested in him and is subject to the same liabilities as if the contract had been made with himself. Section 3 preserves stoppage in transit and the claim for freight. Section 4 makes the bill conclusive evidence of shipment against the signer, subject to fraud and to the holder's actual notice. These re-enact ss.1-3 of the 1856 Act.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (c) names the consignee, and this is the only statute that brings him in. Here the change really is only a citation update.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between a sea waybill and a bill of lading?
retrieval_cards.answer: A sea waybill is a receipt and evidence of the contract but is NOT a document of title. It is non-negotiable, no original need be presented, and delivery is made to the named consignee on proof of identity. It therefore cannot be used to sell the goods in transit or to secure a documentary credit in the same way.
retrieval_cards.why: The waybill is the type most often wrongly described as a kind of bill of lading.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A receiver asks for delivery without an original bill. What is the position?
retrieval_cards.answer: Delivery without production of an original bill is at the carrier's own peril. The carrier remains liable to the true holder of the bill, and a letter of indemnity does not change that - it only gives the carrier a claim against the indemnifier afterwards. Refer to owners and the P&I club; the club form is usually bank-countersigned.
retrieval_cards.why: The most common commercial pressure a master faces, and the answer is not "yes".

retrieval_cards.prompt: What changes about the bill's evidential value when it is transferred?
retrieval_cards.answer: Schedule Article III(4) - the bill is prima facie evidence of receipt of the goods as described, but proof to the contrary is not admissible once the bill has been transferred to a third party acting in good faith. Section 4(1) of the Bills of Lading Act 2025 works to similar effect against the master or other signer.
retrieval_cards.why: The strengthening on transfer is what lets a bank or buyer rely on the document.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name three Indian enacting provisions of the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 2025 that are not in the Schedule.
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 3 - the applicable rules have effect for carriage from any port in India to any other port, whether in or outside India, so the Act bites on outward voyages. Section 4 - there is no implied absolute undertaking of seaworthiness. Section 5 - every bill of lading issued in India must contain an express statement that it takes effect subject to the applicable rules, the statutory clause paramount. Section 12(3) also preserves section 331 and Part XA of the Merchant Shipping Act 1958.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (c) asks for "relevant maritime laws", and the enacting sections are easy marks most candidates miss.

The answer states the 2016 Rules as the current edition and says explicitly that the 1994 or 2004 Rules apply where the bill of lading or charterparty so provides. No claim is made about the market share of any edition at this sitting.

The carrier's lien over cargo for a general average contribution, and the practice of hull underwriters absorbing small general average claims, are commercial and contractual mechanisms outside the York-Antwerp Rules. They are described at the level of practice, and no rule or section is cited for them.
