blocks.h: 1. What general average is, and where the law comes from

blocks.p: General average is the oldest rule in maritime commerce: where something is deliberately sacrificed, or extraordinary expense deliberately incurred, to save a venture in peril, the loss is shared by everyone whose property was saved rather than left with the party who happened to bear it.

Two bodies of law say so, and they are different in kind. The Indian Marine Insurance Act, 1963, section 66(1) defines a general average loss as one caused by or directly consequential on a general average act, and states that it includes a general average expenditure as well as a general average sacrifice. Section 66(3) creates the entitlement: the party on whom the loss falls is entitled, subject to the conditions imposed by maritime law, to a rateable contribution from the other parties interested - the general average contribution.

The York-Antwerp Rules are not a convention and not a statute but a contractual code, applying only because the bill of lading or charterparty incorporates them. The current edition is the YAR 2016, adopted by the Comité Maritime International on 5 May 2016; the 1994 and 2004 Rules still govern contracts that name them, so which edition applies is a question of contract, not of date. Where incorporated, the Rule of Interpretation makes them apply to the exclusion of any law and practice inconsistent therewith.

Contrast particular average, section 64(1): a partial loss caused by a peril insured against which is not a general average loss. It lies where it falls. That distinction - shared against borne alone - is what limb (a) turns on.

blocks.h: 2. The elements of a general average act

blocks.p: Rule A.1 is emphatic in its drafting: there is a general average act "when, and only when" every one of the following is present.

ul: Extraordinary. Ordinary running of the ship, ordinary wear, ordinary consumption of bunkers is not general average. The act must be outside the normal performance of the contract of carriage.
Intentional. A deliberate decision, not the casualty itself. Section 66(2) uses the word voluntarily. Cargo washed overboard is not a jettison.

Reasonable. Both in the decision and in the amount. The Rule Paramount repeats this as an independent override: "In no case shall there be any allowance for sacrifice or expenditure unless reasonably made or incurred."
For the common safety, to preserve from peril. The purpose must be the safety of the whole venture, not of one interest. Section 66(2) says in time of peril.

A common maritime adventure. There must be more than one interest at risk - typically ship, cargo and freight. A ship in ballast on her owner's account cannot declare general average against herself. Rule B extends the idea to vessels towing or pushing one another, provided they are in commercial activity and not in a salvage operation.

blocks.p: Rule A.2 then states the consequence in one line: general average sacrifices and expenditures shall be borne by the different contributing interests on the basis the Rules go on to provide.

blocks.h: 3. What may and may not be allowed

blocks.p: Establishing a general average act does not admit a claim. Four filters apply.

ul: Rule C.1 - directness. Only losses, damages or expenses which are the direct consequence of the act.
Rule C.2 - environment. In no case an allowance for damage to the environment or for the escape or release of pollutant substances. Pollution liability belongs to the pollution regimes.
Rule C.3 - consequential loss. No demurrage, no loss of market, nothing for delay whether on the voyage or afterwards, and no indirect loss whatsoever.
Rule E.1 - proof. The onus is on the party claiming to show the loss is properly allowable.

blocks.p: Three Rules complete the picture. Rule D preserves the right to contribution even where the event was the fault of one of the parties, without prejudice to remedies or defences against that party - so unseaworthiness is fought separately and does not halt the adjustment. Rule F allows a substituted expense incurred in place of an allowable one, but only up to the amount of the general average expense avoided. Rule XIX deals with dishonesty: goods loaded without the shipowner's knowledge or wilfully misdescribed are not allowed yet still contribute if saved; goods declared below their real value are allowed on the declared value but contribute on the actual value.

This is the heart of limb (a). The contributing interests are the ship, the cargo and the freight at risk, each contributing in proportion to its value at the end of the adventure. Rule G.1 fixes the moment: adjustment, as regards both loss and contribution, on values at the time and place when and where the common maritime adventure ends. Rule XVII sets the values:

ul: XVII(a)(i) - contribution on the actual net values of the property at the termination of the common maritime adventure, except cargo, taken at its value at the time of discharge from the commercial invoice rendered to the receiver or, failing that, the shipped value.

XVII(a)(ii) - that value includes insurance and freight unless the freight is at others' risk, and deducts damage suffered before or at discharge. It carries the 2016 innovation: any cargo may be excluded from contributing where the adjuster considers the cost of including it disproportionate to its eventual contribution.

XVII(b) - the amount allowed as general average for property sacrificed is added back, so a party whose goods were sacrificed contributes as if they had been saved. Otherwise sacrifice would be rewarded.
XVII(d) - cargo sold short of destination contributes on the actual net proceeds of sale plus any amount allowed.
XVII(e) - mails, passengers' luggage, accompanied personal effects and accompanied private motor vehicles do not contribute at all.

blocks.p: Two Rules attach further money to the fund. Rule XX allows the capital loss on goods sold to raise funds for general average disbursements, and the cost of insuring those disbursements. Rule XXI allows interest on expenditure, sacrifices and allowances until three months after the date of issue of the adjustment, at the 12-month ICE LIBOR for the currency of the adjustment plus four percentage points - the 2016 Rules having abolished the old 2% commission in its favour.

blocks.h: 5. Security, the adjustment and the time bar

blocks.p: General average is declared by the shipowner, who appoints an average adjuster. The adjuster is not an arbitrator: the adjuster collects values, applies the Rules and issues the adjustment, stating what each interest owes or is owed. The practical lever is cargo - the carrier withholds delivery until security is given, so the receiver signs an average bond and the cargo underwriter issues an average guarantee behind it; where cargo is uninsured a cash deposit is taken. Rule XXIII(a)(i) confirms their standing by referring expressly to rights to claim under general average bonds and guarantees.

ul: Rule XXII - deposits. Sums are remitted forthwith to the adjuster, held in a special account in the adjuster's name, separate from the adjuster's own funds, in trust. Payments on account or refunds need the adjuster's written certificate and the depositor's approval, or ninety days; all are without prejudice to the ultimate liability of the parties.

Rules E.2 and E.3 - information. Every party supplies particulars of value and gives written notice of any claim as soon as possible. After twelve months the adjuster may estimate, and an estimate is challengeable only within two months and only as manifestly incorrect.

Rule XXIII - time bar. Rights to contribution, including under bonds and guarantees, are extinguished unless action is brought within one year of issue of the adjustment, and never more than six years from termination of the adventure. Extendable by agreement; inapplicable between the parties and their own insurers.

blocks.h: 6. Scenarios in which general average is declared

blocks.p: The numbered Rules are, in effect, the examiner's list of examples. Each is a decided category, and quoting the Rule number turns a story into a legal answer.

ul: Jettison of cargo (Rule I) - allowed only if that cargo was carried in accordance with the recognised custom of the trade.
Sacrifice for the common safety (Rule II) - including water going down hatches opened to make a jettison, so cargo never itself sacrificed is still allowed.
Extinguishing fire (Rule III) - water and other fire-fighting damage, including beaching or scuttling a burning ship; but no allowance for damage by smoke however caused, or by heat of the fire.
Voluntary stranding (Rule V) - a ship intentionally run ashore for the common safety, whether or not she might have been driven ashore anyway.

Machinery and boiler damage refloating (Rule VII) - allowed where the ship is ashore and in a position of peril and the damage arose from an actual intention to float her for the common safety at the risk of such damage. Where she is afloat, no such damage is allowed in any circumstances.
Lightening a ship when ashore (Rule VIII) - the extra cost of lightening, lighter hire and reshipping, and consequent damage.
Cargo, materials or stores burnt as fuel (Rule IX) - with credit to general average for the fuel that would otherwise have been consumed.

Port of refuge (Rules X and XI) - entry and departure expenses where the ship put in in consequence of accident, sacrifice or other extraordinary circumstances necessary for the common safety; plus handling, discharging, storage and reloading, and the wages and maintenance of master, officers and crew during the detention.

Salvage remuneration (Rule VI) - allowable where the operation preserved the property from peril; where the parties are separately liable to salvors it is allowed only if one of five conditions applies, and Rule VI(d) excludes article 14 special compensation and SCOPIC altogether.
And the counter-example, Rule IV - cutting away wreck already carried away or effectively lost by accident is not general average. There is nothing left to sacrifice.

blocks.h: 7. Criteria and conditions in modern maritime commerce

blocks.p: Set against any scenario, six conditions decide whether general average applies.

ul: Real peril - real and substantial, though not necessarily immediate. A precaution in fine weather is not general average.
A common adventure - two or more interests must stand to lose. This is why the question says "among parties involved in a maritime venture".
A voluntary act - the casualty is the peril; the response is the act.
Extraordinary and reasonable - separate gates, with the Rule Paramount making reasonableness an override on every allowance.
Success, a saved fund - contribution is levied on values at the end of the adventure (Rules G.1 and XVII). If nothing survives there is nothing to contribute from.
Incorporation - the Rules bind only because the contract of carriage says so; absent that, the position falls back on the general maritime law and, in India, the Marine Insurance Act 1963.

blocks.p: Modern commerce has changed the economics rather than the principle, and the 2016 Rules answer that directly. Containerisation means one casualty can involve thousands of consignees, making security collection disproportionate to the sums recovered - which is why Rule XVII(a)(ii) now lets the adjuster exclude low-value cargo and why Rule E.3 imposes a twelve-month cut-off backed by a power to estimate. Rule C.2 keeps the pollution regimes out of the adjustment, and Rule VI(b) stops salvage being adjusted twice where salvors have been paid separately.

The printed marks are 8 + 8, and the trap is that limb (a) names three things: the concept, the principles, and contribution among the parties. Most candidates write four hundred words on "what is general average" and then run out of time before contribution - which is the part the examiner has singled out and which no textbook paragraph covers. Route steps 1 to 3 handle the concept and principles briskly; steps 4 and 5 spend the marks where the question points.

Limb (b) asks for two things at once - examples and criteria and conditions. Splitting them into steps 6 and 7 means neither is dropped. Step 6 is a list of Rules; step 7 is the reasoning that governs all of them.

blocks.h: Statute, contract, convention - keep the three apart

blocks.p: General average is unusual in that the instrument students quote most - the York-Antwerp Rules - has no legislative force at all. It is a set of contractual terms produced by a private international body, the CMI, and binds only where a bill of lading or charterparty incorporates it. The Marine Insurance Act 1963 is the Indian statute, and it governs the insurance relationship - what the assured may recover from the underwriter - as much as the adjustment itself.

This matters practically. If asked "which York-Antwerp Rules apply to this casualty?", the answer is whichever edition the contract names. A 2025 casualty under a bill of lading referring to the YAR 1994 is adjusted on the 1994 Rules. Saying "the 2016 Rules, because they are the latest" is wrong.

blocks.h: What changed in 2016, and why it is worth knowing

ul: Rule VI (salvage). The 2004 Rules had removed salvage from general average and were consequently almost never used. The 2016 Rules restore it, subject to the five gateways at VI(b) which prevent pointless re-adjustment where salvors have been paid separately.

Rules X, XI and XIV. The 1994 wording for port of refuge expenses, crew wages and temporary repairs was retained - the main reason shipowners accepted the 2016 Rules where they had rejected the 2004 Rules.
Rule XVII. The low-value cargo exclusion is new, and is the clearest example of the Rules bending to container economics.
Rules XX and XXI. The old 2% commission on general average disbursements was abolished, replaced by interest at 12-month ICE LIBOR + 4 percentage points.

blocks.p: BIMCO agreed in May 2016 that its charterparties and bills of lading should refer to the 2016 Rules, which is how the edition spread into standard forms.

ul: Writing the history of the Rhodian law and Lex Mercatoria. It earns nothing. The examiner asked for principles and contribution.
Answering limb (a) without ever reaching contribution. Half the limb is about who pays what.
Saying general average is "a convention" or "IMO law". It is neither.
Forgetting that sacrificed property still contributes (Rule XVII(b)). Candidates routinely say the jettisoned cargo owner "is paid and contributes nothing".
Treating fire damage as wholly allowable. Smoke and heat damage are excluded by Rule III - they are the peril, not the sacrifice.
Claiming machinery damage in general average for a ship that is afloat. Rule VII excludes it in any circumstances.
Saying fault defeats general average. Rule D says the opposite - the adjustment proceeds and fault is fought separately.
"Only when". Rule A.1 uses those words. Every element must be present; the examiner is testing whether you know it is a conjunctive test.
Voluntary versus accidental. Cargo washed overboard is a particular average loss; cargo jettisoned is general average. Same cargo, same sea.
Rule IV. Cutting away a mast already carried away is not a sacrifice - a favourite oral question.
Rule XVII(e). Mails, passengers' luggage, accompanied personal effects and accompanied private motor vehicles do not contribute. Easy marks, rarely given.
The two time limits. Rule E.3's twelve months for particulars of value is not the same thing as Rule XXIII's one year from the adjustment, six years absolute.
SCOPIC. Rule VI(d) puts article 14 special compensation and SCOPIC outside general average.

"Your ship grounds and you damage the main engine trying to refloat. Is that general average?" - Rule VII: yes if she was ashore and in peril and the damage arose from an actual intention to refloat for the common safety; no if she was afloat.
"Who declares general average, and who pays the adjuster?" - the shipowner declares and appoints; the adjuster's fee is a general average disbursement borne by the fund.
"What is the difference between an average bond and an average guarantee?" - the bond is given by the cargo receiver, the guarantee by the cargo underwriter backing it.
"Can you refuse to deliver cargo until security is given?" - yes, that is the practical basis on which security is collected.
"The grounding was caused by our own negligent navigation. Can we still claim?" - Rule D: rights to contribution are unaffected, without prejudice to defences against us.
"Give three items that do not contribute." - Rule XVII(e).
"What is a substituted expense?" - Rule F, capped at the general average expense avoided; towage to destination in place of repairs at a port of refuge is the standard illustration.

blocks.p: For the elements, hold five words in Rule A order: EXTRAORDINARY, INTENTIONAL, REASONABLE, COMMON SAFETY, COMMON ADVENTURE - then add SAVED, because contribution is levied on what survives. Six gates, and every scenario in limb (b) is tested against them.

For contribution, remember the sequence VALUE - ADD BACK - EXCLUDE - APPORTION: take the actual net value at the end of the adventure (Rule XVII(a)); add back what was sacrificed (XVII(b)); exclude what does not contribute (XVII(e), and uneconomic cargo under XVII(a)(ii)); apportion the fund rateably (s.66(3), Rule A.2).

ul: Marine Insurance Act 1963 s.66(1) - definition; s.66(2) - the general average act; s.66(3) - rateable contribution; s.66(4)-(5) - recovery from the insurer.
s.64(1) - particular average is a partial loss that is not general average.
YAR 2016 Rule of Interpretation and Rule Paramount - precedence, and reasonableness as an override.
Rule A - the act and the sharing. Rule B - towage and pushing.
Rule C - directness; environment; delay. Rule D - fault. Rule E - proof, particulars, twelve months. Rule F - substituted expenses. Rule G - time and place of adjustment.
Rules I-XI - the allowable categories: jettison, sacrifice, fire, wreck, stranding, salvage, machinery, lightening, fuel, port of refuge, wages.
Rule XVII - contributory values, including the low-value exclusion and the non-contributing interests.
Rules XIX-XXIII - misdeclared cargo, provision of funds, interest, cash deposits, time bar.

blocks.h: The scenarios in longer form - detail behind route step 6

blocks.p: The Model Answer states each category as a proposition plus its Rule number, which is what scores. The colour below is for the oral and for reading around the topic.

ul: Jettison. The custom-of-the-trade condition in Rule I is aimed squarely at deck cargo. Containers stowed on deck under a modern trade where deck carriage is customary are within the Rule; goods stowed on deck against the custom of that trade are not, and their jettison earns no allowance.

Fire. Rule III draws the sharpest line in the Rules between peril damage and sacrifice damage. The water you put on the fire is a sacrifice; the smoke and the heat are the casualty. Beaching or scuttling a burning ship is expressly on the sacrifice side, which is why a deliberate flooding decision is worth recording carefully in the engine room log and the deck log alike.

Refloating. Rule VII is the one a Chief Engineer meets in practice. Working the main engine hard astern with the ship aground, knowing the risk to bearings, tailshaft, boilers or coolers, is a classic general average sacrifice - provided the ship was in a position of peril and the intention is evidenced. The engine-room record of the order, the times, the loads and the reason is what proves that intention months later, and its absence is the usual reason such a claim fails.

Port of refuge. This is the largest single head of general average expenditure in practice, because Rules X and XI between them pick up entry, discharge, storage, reloading, departure, and crew wages and maintenance for the whole detention. Rule X(a)(ii) extends the same treatment to a second port where repairs cannot be done at the first, including temporary repairs and towage.

Salvage. The five gateways at Rule VI(b) exist because, where every interest has already settled with the salvors under its own Lloyd's Open Form apportionment, putting salvage back through the general average adjustment usually moves very little money and costs a great deal. The gateways admit it only where it makes a real difference - for example where there are significant general average sacrifices, or where salved values are manifestly incorrect.

blocks.p: The York-Antwerp Rules 2016 were read from the International Group of P&I Clubs' published copy of the CMI text. The Rules are a private code and there is no official gazette; this is the standard circulated text and matched the club circular describing the 2016 changes.

The Marine Insurance Act 1963 was read from a complete third-party reproduction of the Act, because India Code refuses automated retrieval. The section 66 wording used here matches that reproduction and the section as summarised on India Code and Indian Kanoon. Nothing in the answer turns on a fine point of statutory wording; the reliance is on section numbers and substance.

The carrier's right to withhold delivery pending security, and the practice of average bonds and guarantees, are described at the level of commercial practice. They are not created by the York-Antwerp Rules, although Rule XXIII(a)(i) assumes their existence. No rule or section is cited for them.

notes: Intake said STABLE / LOW. CONFIRMED on evidence at authoring rather than inherited.

York-Antwerp Rules 2016 re-confirmed as the current edition at this sitting; the CMI has adopted no later set. The CMI Guidelines Relating to General Average were re-issued in a 2nd edition in 2022, but they expressly do not form part of the Rules, are not binding and override nothing - no proposition in the answer moves.
Marine Insurance Act 1963 sections 64 to 66 unamended and in force at this sitting.

STRUCTURAL REASON THE RISK IS LOW: which edition of the Rules applies is CONTRACTUAL - whichever edition the bill of lading or charterparty names - so the answer's central caution ('the latest edition does not apply automatically') is itself time-proof.
One sitting-relative edit only: a worked example dated to the donor year was re-dated. No legal proposition changed.

steps.title: What general average is, and where the law comes from
points: Marine Insurance Act 1963 s.66(1) - a loss caused by or directly consequential on a general average act
s.66(1) - it includes a general average expenditure as well as a general average sacrifice
s.66(3) - the party on whom it falls is entitled to a rateable contribution from the other parties interested
that rateable share is the general average contribution
the York-Antwerp Rules are CONTRACTUAL - they apply because the bill of lading or charterparty says so
YAR 2016 adopted by the CMI on 5 May 2016; the 1994 and 2004 Rules still govern where the contract so provides
Rule of Interpretation - the Rules apply to the exclusion of any inconsistent law and practice
contrast s.64(1) - particular average is a partial loss that is NOT general average, and lies where it falls

steps.title: The elements of a general average act
points: Rule A.1 - there is a general average act when, and ONLY when, five things are true
the sacrifice or expenditure must be EXTRAORDINARY
it must be made INTENTIONALLY - s.66(2) says voluntarily
it must be REASONABLE - and the Rule Paramount repeats it as an override
it must be for the COMMON SAFETY, to preserve from peril
the property must be involved in a COMMON MARITIME ADVENTURE - more than one interest at risk
Rule A.2 - the loss is borne by the different contributing interests
Rule B - vessels towing or pushing in commercial activity can form one adventure

steps.title: What may and may not be allowed
points: Rule C.1 - only the DIRECT consequence of the general average act
Rule C.2 - nothing for damage to the environment or escape of pollutants
Rule C.3 - no demurrage, no loss of market, no delay loss, no indirect loss
Rule Paramount - nothing at all unless reasonably made or incurred
Rule E.1 - the onus of proof is on the party claiming
Rule D - fault does not defeat the right to contribute, without prejudice to remedies
Rule F - a substituted expense is allowed, capped at the general average expense avoided
Rule XIX - undeclared or misdescribed cargo is not allowed, but still contributes if saved

steps.title: Contribution among the parties
points: the contributing interests are ship, cargo and freight at risk
Rule G.1 - values at the time and place where the common maritime adventure ends
Rule XVII(a)(i) - actual net values at termination; cargo at its value at time of discharge
cargo value from the commercial invoice to the receiver, or the shipped value
Rule XVII(a)(ii) - value includes insurance and freight, less pre-discharge damage
Rule XVII(a)(ii) - low-value cargo MAY be excluded if inclusion would cost more than it contributes
Rule XVII(b) - add back the amount allowed as general average for property sacrificed
Rule XVII(e) - mails, passengers luggage, accompanied personal effects and accompanied private cars do NOT contribute
Rule XX - capital loss on goods sold to raise funds, and the cost of insuring disbursements
Rule XXI - interest to three months after the adjustment, at 12-month ICE LIBOR plus four percentage points

steps.title: Security, the adjustment and the time bar
points: the shipowner declares general average and appoints an average adjuster
cargo is not released until security is given - that is the practical lever
a general average BOND from the cargo receiver, and a general average GUARANTEE from the cargo underwriter
Rule XXIII(a)(i) recognises rights to claim under general average bonds and guarantees
Rule XXII - a cash deposit goes to a special account in the adjuster's name, held in trust
Rule XXII(c) - refunds or payments on account need the depositor's approval, or ninety days
Rule E.2 - all parties supply particulars of value as soon as possible, in writing
Rule E.3 - twelve months, after which the adjuster may estimate; estimates challengeable within two months
Rule XXIII - one year from issue of the adjustment, and never more than six years from the end of the adventure

steps.title: Scenarios in which general average is declared
points: Rule I - jettison of cargo, but only if carried per the recognised custom of the trade
Rule II - water damage down hatches opened to make a jettison
Rule III - fire fighting damage, including beaching or scuttling a burning ship
Rule III - but NOT damage by smoke however caused, nor by heat of the fire
Rule V - voluntary stranding for the common safety
Rule VII - machinery and boiler damage refloating a ship ashore and in peril - never when afloat
Rule VIII - lightening a ship when ashore, lighter hire and reshipping
Rule IX - cargo, materials or stores burnt as fuel for the common safety
Rule X and XI - port of refuge: entry and departure expenses, discharge, storage, wages and maintenance
Rule VI - salvage remuneration, but Rule VI(d) excludes article 14 special compensation and SCOPIC
Rule IV - cutting away wreck already lost by accident is NOT general average

steps.title: Criteria and conditions in modern maritime commerce
points: the peril must be real and substantial, though it need not be immediate
there must be a genuine common adventure - one interest alone cannot average
the act must be a choice, not the accident itself
there must be a saved fund - property must survive to carry a contributory value
the York-Antwerp Rules must be incorporated by the contract of carriage
containerisation makes security collection from many consignees slow and costly
that pressure is why Rule XVII(a)(ii) now lets the adjuster exclude uneconomic cargo
Rule C.2 keeps pollution liability out of general average and inside the pollution regimes
Rule VI(b) stops salvage being adjusted twice when salvors are separately paid
the practical test in the exam: extraordinary, intentional, reasonable, common safety, common adventure, saved

questions.understand_first: General average is a loss-sharing rule, not an insurance product and not a safety regulation. One party deliberately gives something up so that everyone's property survives; the law then makes everyone whose property survived pay a share. Two sources say so, and they are different in kind: the Marine Insurance Act 1963 is Indian statute, and the York-Antwerp Rules are a contractual code that binds only because the bill of lading incorporates it. The half that gets dropped is contribution - who pays, and how much. The logic is only proportion: everyone whose property arrived safely owes a share measured by what that property was worth on arrival, because that value is the measure of what the sacrifice bought them. Once that is clear, testing a real casualty becomes a single repeated question, asked of each item of damage - was this deliberately incurred to save the whole, or merely suffered along the way?
questions.memory_cue: Six gates decide every general average question, and they are route steps 2 and 7: EXTRAORDINARY, INTENTIONAL, REASONABLE, COMMON SAFETY, COMMON ADVENTURE, SAVED (2, 7). Then the money follows four moves in route step 4: VALUE, ADD BACK, EXCLUDE, APPORTION (4).

quick_revision.recall_15s: Marine Insurance Act 1963 s.66(1): a general average loss is caused by or directly consequential on a general average act, and includes expenditure as well as sacrifice. s.66(3): the party on whom it falls gets a rateable contribution from the other parties interested. York-Antwerp Rules 2016 are CONTRACTUAL - they apply because the bill of lading says so. Rule A.1: extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure, intentionally and reasonably made, for the common safety, to preserve property in a common maritime adventure. Rule C: direct consequence only, nothing for environment or delay. Rule D: fault does not defeat contribution. Rule G.1 and Rule XVII: contribution on actual net values where the adventure ends, cargo at time of discharge, sacrificed property added back, mails and passengers' effects excluded. Rule XXIII: one year from the adjustment, six years absolute.

quick_revision.critical_regulation: York-Antwerp Rules 2016, Rule A.1 - there is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure. Read it with Rule XVII, which sets the contributory values, and with section 66 of the Marine Insurance Act 1963.
quick_revision.major_trap: Answering limb (a) without reaching contribution among the parties. The examiner named it expressly and it is where Rule XVII lives - actual net values at the end of the adventure, cargo at time of discharge, sacrificed property ADDED BACK so it still contributes, and mails, passengers' luggage, accompanied personal effects and accompanied private motor vehicles excluded entirely.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the general average question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What it is and where the law comes from. 2 (a) The elements of a general average act. 3 (a) What may and may not be allowed. 4 (a) Contribution among the parties. 5 (a) Security, adjustment and time bar. 6 (b) Scenarios. 7 (b) Criteria and conditions in modern commerce.
retrieval_cards.why: Steps 4 and 5 are the half of limb (a) most candidates never reach.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define a general average act in the words of Rule A.1.
retrieval_cards.answer: There is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure.
retrieval_cards.why: "When, and only when" signals a conjunctive test - every element must be present.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does section 66 of the Marine Insurance Act 1963 provide?
retrieval_cards.answer: s.66(1) a general average loss is caused by or directly consequential on a general average act and includes expenditure as well as sacrifice; s.66(2) the act is an extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure voluntarily and reasonably made in time of peril to preserve the property imperilled in the common adventure; s.66(3) the party on whom it falls is entitled to a rateable contribution from the other parties interested.
retrieval_cards.why: The statutory limb of the answer - the York-Antwerp Rules are not legislation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why are the York-Antwerp Rules not a convention, and what follows from that?
retrieval_cards.answer: They are a private contractual code produced by the CMI. They bind only where the bill of lading or charterparty incorporates them, so which edition applies - 1994, 2004 or 2016 - is decided by the contract, not by the date of the casualty. Where incorporated, the Rule of Interpretation makes them apply to the exclusion of any inconsistent law and practice.
retrieval_cards.why: A very common error is to assert the latest edition applies automatically.

retrieval_cards.prompt: On what basis is the contribution calculated?
retrieval_cards.answer: Rule G.1 - on values at the time and place where the common maritime adventure ends. Rule XVII(a)(i) - actual net values of the property at termination, except cargo, taken at its value at time of discharge from the commercial invoice to the receiver or the shipped value. Rule XVII(b) - the amount allowed as general average for property sacrificed is added back, so sacrificed property still contributes.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the "contribution among parties" the question names expressly.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which interests do not contribute to general average?
retrieval_cards.answer: Rule XVII(e) - mails, passengers' luggage, accompanied personal effects and accompanied private motor vehicles. Separately, under Rule XVII(a)(ii) the adjuster may exclude any cargo where the cost of including it would be disproportionate to its eventual contribution.
retrieval_cards.why: Four exact categories, plus the 2016 discretionary exclusion.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The grounding was caused by the shipowner's own negligent navigation. Does general average still apply?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes. Rule D - rights to contribution are not affected though the event was due to the fault of one of the parties, but this is without prejudice to any remedies or defences open against that party. The adjustment proceeds; fault is litigated separately.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates routinely say fault destroys the claim. It does not.

retrieval_cards.prompt: You damage the main engine trying to refloat. When is that general average?
retrieval_cards.answer: Rule VII - damage to machinery and boilers is allowed when the ship is ashore and in a position of peril and the damage is shown to have arisen from an actual intention to float her for the common safety at the risk of such damage. Where the ship is afloat, no loss or damage from working the propelling machinery and boilers is allowed in any circumstances.
retrieval_cards.why: The engineering scenario most likely to be put to a Chief Engineer orally.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between an average bond and an average guarantee?
retrieval_cards.answer: The average bond is given by the cargo receiver, undertaking to pay the contribution once adjusted and to supply the values the adjuster needs. The average guarantee is given by the cargo underwriter to back that undertaking. Where cargo is uninsured a cash deposit is taken instead, and Rule XXII requires it to be held in a special account in the adjuster's name, separate from the adjuster's own funds.
retrieval_cards.why: Security is how the contribution is actually collected before cargo is released.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the general average time bar.
retrieval_cards.answer: Rule XXIII(a)(i) - rights to contribution, including under general average bonds and guarantees, are extinguished unless action is brought within one year after the date the adjustment is issued, and in no case more than six years from termination of the common maritime adventure. Extendable by agreement, and not applicable between the parties and their own insurers.
retrieval_cards.why: Two limits, and they are commonly confused with Rule E.3's twelve months.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Fire on board. Which fire damage is general average and which is not?
retrieval_cards.answer: Rule III - damage done to ship and cargo by water or otherwise in extinguishing the fire, including damage by beaching or scuttling a burning ship, is allowed. But no allowance is made for damage by smoke however caused, or by heat of the fire - that is damage by the peril, not by the sacrifice.
retrieval_cards.why: The clearest illustration of the sacrifice-versus-peril line.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a substituted expense?
retrieval_cards.answer: Rule F - any additional expense incurred in place of another expense which would have been allowable as general average is deemed to be general average and allowed without regard to any saving to other interests, but only up to the amount of the general average expense avoided.
retrieval_cards.why: The cap is the examinable part, and it is routinely omitted.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two limbs of eight marks. Limb (a) names THREE tasks - concept, underlying principles, and contribution among the parties - and the third is the one that distinguishes this question from every other general average question in the corpus. Limb (b) asks for worked scenarios AND the criteria and conditions for application in modern maritime commerce, so a bare list of examples does not answer it.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16 marks printed as 8 + 8. Within limb (a) the practical split is roughly three marks for concept and principles and five for contribution and its machinery, because contribution is named expressly and is the harder half.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate can name Rules rather than describe stories. The tells are Rule A's "when, and only when", Rule XVII's contributory values with the add-back of sacrificed property, Rule XVII(e)'s non-contributing interests, Rule D on fault, and Rule VII on machinery damage when ashore against afloat.
primary_source_plan: Read the York-Antwerp Rules 2016 themselves, not a summary of the changes
Read the lettered Rules A to G in full - they carry the principles
Read Rule XVII in full - it carries contribution, which is what the question weights
Read Rules I to XI for the scenarios, and note the counter-examples at III and IV
Read Marine Insurance Act 1963 sections 64 to 66 for the Indian statutory position
Establish which changes the 2016 edition made, from a club circular rather than by inference
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: LOW. The York-Antwerp Rules 2016 were re-confirmed at authoring as the current edition at this sitting - the CMI has adopted no later set, and the CMI Guidelines Relating to General Average (2nd edition, 2022) are guidance that expressly does not form part of the Rules. Which edition applies is in any event contractual, not chronological. The Marine Insurance Act 1963 is unamended and in force throughout.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: MODERATE and handled. The question is set in India, so the Indian statute is cited rather than the UK Marine Insurance Act 1906 which most textbooks quote. The two are closely parallel, but citing the wrong statute in an Indian examination is avoidable.
technical_ambiguities: Whether the York-Antwerp Rules are law or contract - they are contract
Whether sacrificed property contributes - it does, by add-back under Rule XVII(b)
Whether fault defeats the claim - it does not, Rule D
Whether success is required - contribution is levied on values at the end of the adventure
Whether machinery damage refloating is always allowed - only when ashore and in peril
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Concept and legal sources first, because the statute-versus-contract distinction frames everything; then the elements and the filters; then contribution and its machinery, which is where limb (a)'s weight sits; then the scenarios Rule by Rule; then the criteria that test any scenario, closing on what modern commerce changed.
decomposition_gate.note: Command verbs -> command_verbs. Required answer components -> decomposition. Internal reuse map -> reuse_evidence. Not duplicated here.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The York-Antwerp Rules 2016 are the current edition at the October 2025 sitting
reverify_before_publication.why: Anchored to the sitting date. The CMI reviews the Rules periodically and a later edition would not change the analysis but would change the "current edition" statement. Re-confirmed at authoring that no edition later than 2016 had been adopted before October 2025. Confirm again before publication.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The Marine Insurance Act 1963 section 66 wording relied on
reverify_before_publication.why: Read from a complete third-party reproduction of the Act because India Code refuses automated retrieval. Not blocking: the wording was corroborated against the section as summarised on India Code and Indian Kanoon, and it is the long-settled statutory formula. Nothing in the answer turns on fine wording. Confirm against an India Code or Gazette copy before publication so the citation rests on an official text.

reverify_before_publication.claim: Rule XXI's interest rate is 12-month ICE LIBOR plus four percentage points
reverify_before_publication.why: The Rule is quoted as printed in the 2016 text. LIBOR has been withdrawn as a published benchmark since the Rules were drafted, and market practice has moved to successor rates. The Rule as printed is what the answer states; how it is applied in practice was not researched and is not asserted.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The carrier may withhold delivery of cargo until general average security is provided
reverify_before_publication.why: Stated as commercial practice and as the assumption behind Rule XXIII(a)(i)'s reference to bonds and guarantees. It is a contractual and common-law lien question, not a York-Antwerp Rule, and no authority is cited for it.

blocks.h: 1. Why propeller efficiency is worth pursuing

blocks.p: The propeller is the final energy conversion in the propulsion chain and one of the least efficient links in it: a large proportion of the delivered power never becomes useful thrust. Because resistance rises steeply with speed, a modest improvement in propulsive efficiency releases a disproportionate saving in fuel and therefore in emissions.

The stem supplies its own framing - "improving efficiency of propellers is recognized as a growing means to improve energy efficiency of ships" - and that framing is sound at this sitting, because ship energy efficiency requirements, technical and operational, were already in force. A propeller change has a particular attraction in that context: it improves the ship's technical efficiency and her measured operational performance at the same time, and unlike reducing speed it costs the operator no time.

A useful answer explains what each device is attacking before describing it. Overall propulsive efficiency is the product of hull efficiency, open-water (propeller) efficiency and relative rotative efficiency. The devices in this question act chiefly on the second, where the energy is lost in four ways:

ul: Axial or slipstream loss. The propeller works by accelerating water aft; the kinetic energy left in that accelerated column is lost. It falls as the disc area is increased and the acceleration reduced.

Rotational loss. A single propeller leaves the race rotating. That swirl carries energy which does nothing to propel the ship, and it is the largest single recoverable loss in a conventional installation.
Frictional loss. Viscous drag over the blade surfaces - irreducible, and worsened by roughness and fouling.

Tip vortex loss. At the blade tip the pressure difference between face and back equalises around the edge, shedding a strong vortex which carries away energy and is a principal source of pressure pulses, hull vibration and cavitation erosion.

blocks.p: Cavitation sets the ceiling. Blade loading cannot simply be increased, because local pressure falling to vapour pressure produces cavities whose collapse causes erosion, vibration and noise. Every device below is an attempt to recover one of these losses without breaching that ceiling: the duct attacks axial loss and tip loss, Kappel attacks tip vortex loss, and contra-rotation attacks rotational loss.

Principle. The propeller runs inside an annular aerofoil - a nozzle, the classic form being the Kort nozzle. In an accelerating duct the internal section converges, so flow is accelerated into the disc; each blade then has to generate less thrust for the same total, and the duct itself, being a lifting surface with circulation, produces additional forward thrust. The close tip clearance also largely suppresses the tip vortex. A decelerating duct reverses the section to raise pressure at the disc and suppress cavitation and radiated noise - mainly a naval application.

The governing parameter is thrust loading. The duct earns its keep where the propeller is heavily loaded at low speed: tugs, trawlers, pushers, and slow, full-form ships whose diameter is limited by draught.

ul: Merits. Substantial thrust augmentation at high loading, which is why bollard pull vessels are almost universally ducted; improved efficiency where the propeller would otherwise be overloaded; suppression of tip vortex and its associated erosion; physical protection of the propeller from debris and quay contact; improved course stability with a fixed nozzle; and, with a steerable nozzle, a genuine manoeuvring gain that can remove the need for a separate rudder.

Demerits. The duct is an appendage with its own drag, and at light loading and higher speed that drag exceeds the benefit - a duct can make a fast, lightly loaded ship worse. It fouls and corrodes, and marine growth inside the nozzle degrades performance quickly; it can be damaged or blocked by debris or ice; internal cavitation erosion occurs on the inner surface and at the tip gap; clearances are critical and alignment must be maintained; it adds weight and structure; and it complicates survey, inspection and propeller removal in dry dock.

blocks.p: Principle. A Kappel propeller is a conventional-diameter propeller whose blade tips are curved smoothly towards the suction side, forming an integrated, continuous winglet rather than a bolted-on end plate. The curvature allows blade loading to be carried further outboard while the tip vortex is weakened and displaced away from the blade. The aeronautical analogy is exact: it is the marine equivalent of an aircraft winglet, and it recovers energy from the same mechanism.

ul: Merits. It reduces tip vortex loss for the same diameter, which matters when draught or aperture fixes the diameter. There is no additional appendage, so no added drag, no added fouling surface and no new maintenance item. The weakened tip vortex produces a more uniform wake into the rudder, reducing pressure pulses, hull vibration and radiated noise - a real habitability and structural benefit as well as an efficiency one. And it is retrofittable as a straight propeller replacement at a scheduled dry docking.

Demerits. The gain is modest and is highly dependent on the hull wake field, so it must be designed for the specific ship - which means CFD and model testing, and a high design cost that is hard to justify on a single vessel. The curved tip geometry is complex to cast, dearer than a conventional blade, and more difficult to repair, straighten or re-pitch after damage; the tip is also relatively vulnerable. Finally, the benefit is design-point dependent - a ship trading persistently away from the draught and speed for which the blade was designed may realise little of it.

blocks.p: Principle. Two propellers are mounted coaxially on the same axis and turn in opposite directions. The forward propeller leaves a rotating race; the after propeller, turning the other way, is designed to recover that rotational energy and convert it into additional thrust. Because rotational loss is the largest single recoverable loss in a conventional installation, this attacks the biggest target directly. Mechanically it requires either coaxial inner and outer shafting with epicyclic gearing, or a podded after unit driven electrically in the hybrid arrangement.

ul: Merits. The highest theoretical efficiency gain of the three, because it recovers swirl rather than merely avoiding a loss. The total thrust is divided between two propellers, so loading per propeller falls - which reduces cavitation risk, pressure pulses and induced vibration, and permits a smaller diameter for a given thrust, valuable where draught constrains the aperture. Torque reaction is largely cancelled, improving course keeping and reducing rudder correction.

Demerits. The objection is mechanical, and it is serious. The arrangement demands concentric inner and outer shafting with complex reduction and reversing gearing, and the sealing of two concentric shafts at the stern tube is a recognised reliability weak point. Capital cost is high; alignment, maintenance, and dry-dock withdrawal are all substantially harder; there are more components to fail in a system whose failure immobilises the ship. Service experience in the large merchant fleet remains limited, so spares support and operator confidence lag the theory - which, more than the engineering, is why adoption has been slow.

blocks.h: 6. Choosing between them, and the printed demand

blocks.p: The three are not competitors for the same ship. The choice follows the thrust loading coefficient and the operating profile:

ul: Heavily loaded, low speed, high thrust - tug, trawler, pusher, slow full-form ship: the duct earns its drag several times over.
Moderately loaded single screw with a reasonably clean wake: a tip-modified blade such as Kappel gives a real gain with no new appendage and no new maintenance.
Where rotational loss is large and mechanical complexity is acceptable: contra-rotating offers the most, at the highest engineering and commercial risk.
Lightly loaded and fast: a duct is likely to make the ship worse, and this is the trap in the question - a device is not "high efficiency" in the abstract.

blocks.p: Two points on answering. The stem asks for any three of the four, with merits and demerits. Three treated properly earns more than four treated superficially, and an answer that gives only merits has answered half the question. And give no percentage figures: published gains are manufacturer-sourced and depend entirely on hull form, wake field, loading and trade. A correctly explained mechanism is worth more than a number you cannot defend.

The question prints no mark allocation and asks for three of four devices with merits and demerits. That is effectively four equal blocks of about four marks: one for the framing and the loss mechanisms, and one for each device. Route steps 1 and 2 are the framing; steps 3, 4 and 5 are the three devices in the printed order; step 6 is the comparative judgement that turns three descriptions into a discussion.

Step 2 is what separates a Class I answer from a Class II one. Anyone can describe a nozzle. Explaining that a propeller loses energy axially, rotationally, frictionally and at the tip, and that each device attacks a different one of those, gives the whole answer a spine and makes the merits and demerits follow logically instead of being recited.
The Model Answer takes ducted, Kappel and contra-rotating, which is the printed demand of three. If you would rather substitute azimuth propulsion for one of them, here is the same treatment.

Principle. The propeller is carried in a steerable unit that rotates about a vertical axis, so thrust can be directed through a full circle. Drive is either mechanical through bevel gearing in a Z-drive, or electrical to a motor housed in a submerged pod. In a pulling (tractor) configuration the propeller runs ahead of the pod, in undisturbed inflow, which is the main hydrodynamic advantage.

ul: Merits. The propeller works in a clean, uniform wake rather than in the hull's disturbed boundary layer, which improves efficiency and reduces cavitation and vibration; no rudder, no long shaft line, no stern tube and no separate reversing arrangement; outstanding manoeuvrability with full thrust in any direction and strong crash-stop performance; freed hull volume forward of the pod for cargo or machinery; and, with diesel-electric drive, the prime movers can be loaded efficiently and sited flexibly.

Demerits. High capital cost and dependence on the electrical chain, so a switchboard, converter or motor fault removes propulsion; the pod is a submerged, largely inaccessible unit, so significant repair usually means dry docking and specialist attendance; slewing bearings and seals are highly loaded and are the recognised failure mode; appendage drag of the pod and strut partly offsets the inflow benefit at higher speeds; conversion losses through the electrical chain; and crew familiarity and spares support are less widespread than for conventional shafting.
Describing all four superficially when the stem asked for three. This is the single commonest error on this question.
Giving merits only. The stem says merits and demerits; half the marks are in the second half.
Quoting percentage gains. Vendor figures, hull-specific, indefensible under questioning.
Saying a duct always improves efficiency. It does not - at light loading its drag makes the ship worse. Loading is the whole story.
Confusing Kappel with a bolted-on end plate or a tip fin. It is an integrated blade geometry.
Treating contra-rotating as merely "two propellers". The point is recovery of rotational energy.
Omitting cavitation, which is the constraint that makes all of this difficult.
Thrust loading decides everything about a duct. If you can state that, you have shown you understand rather than remember.
Accelerating against decelerating ducts. The second exists for cavitation and noise, not for efficiency.
The vibration benefit. Kappel and contra-rotation both reduce pressure pulses into the hull - an easy extra mark that connects to habitability and structural fatigue.
The stern tube seal on concentric shafting. The most credible practical objection to contra-rotating propellers, and a Chief Engineer is expected to raise it.
Design point. Every one of these devices is optimised for a condition; a ship trading away from it realises less.
"Why is a tug ducted and a container ship not?" - thrust loading. High loading at low speed is where the accelerating duct pays; at light loading its drag dominates.
"What is the largest recoverable loss in a conventional propeller?" - the rotational loss left in the race, which is what contra-rotation targets.
"How does a winglet on a propeller help?" - it weakens and displaces the tip vortex, reducing the energy shed at the tip and the pressure pulses into the hull.
"What limits how hard you can load a blade?" - cavitation, and its erosion, vibration and noise consequences.

"What would you inspect on a ducted propeller in dry dock?" - tip clearance and duct alignment, internal erosion at the tip gap, fouling and coating condition, structural attachment and any debris damage.

"You are offered a propeller retrofit. How would you justify it?" - measured hull and propeller performance data before and after, separating the effect from weather, loading and fouling. This links directly to Q1.

blocks.p: Four losses, three devices: AXIAL, ROTATIONAL, FRICTIONAL, TIP. The duct attacks axial and tip; Kappel attacks tip; contra-rotation attacks rotational. Nothing usefully attacks frictional except cleanliness. If you hold that one sentence you can reconstruct the whole answer, including why a duct is wrong for a fast ship.

No instrument prescribes a propeller type, and none is cited. The regulatory connection is indirect: ship energy efficiency requirements, technical and operational, were in force before this sitting and are what make propeller efficiency a compliance matter as well as a commercial one. The Model Answer states that connection without regulation numbers, deliberately - see below.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the limits of this answer

blocks.p: This is an engineering question and the answer says so. The hydrodynamics - the decomposition of propulsive efficiency, the four loss mechanisms, the loading-dependence of duct benefit, the tip vortex and the cavitation ceiling - is settled naval architecture and is explained mechanistically rather than cited.

No percentage efficiency gain is quoted anywhere in this answer, for any device. Published figures vary widely, depend entirely on hull form, wake field, loading and operating profile, and originate largely from manufacturers. This is a deliberate decision, recorded so that a later editor does not "improve" the answer by adding them.

The MARPOL Annex VI energy efficiency provisions were not read in a licensed consolidated edition for this question. The Model Answer therefore refers to the regulatory driver in general terms and asserts no regulation number and no date. If a future revision wishes to cite EEXI or CII by regulation, the Annex must be read first.

questions.understand_first: This is a physics question dressed as a list. Every one of these devices exists to recover ONE of the ways a propeller wastes energy - axially in the slipstream, rotationally as swirl, frictionally on the blades, and at the tip as a shed vortex - without crossing the cavitation limit. The duct attacks axial and tip loss, Kappel attacks tip loss, contra-rotation attacks rotational loss. Once you hold that, the merits and demerits stop being a list to memorise and become consequences you can derive. The other half of the question is discipline: the stem asks for THREE of four, with merits AND demerits, and gives no marks for a fourth device or for unbalanced praise.
questions.memory_cue: Four losses - AXIAL, ROTATIONAL, FRICTIONAL, TIP - are set out in route step 2. Then each device attacks one: DUCT takes axial and tip (3), KAPPEL takes tip (4), CONTRA takes rotational (5). Choose by loading in route step 6.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Propulsive efficiency = hull x open-water x relative rotative. Open-water losses are axial (slipstream), rotational (swirl), frictional (blade drag) and tip vortex; cavitation caps blade loading. Ducted: an annular aerofoil accelerating flow, generating its own thrust and closing the tip gap - excellent at high thrust loading and low speed, a net penalty at light loading because of appendage drag, plus fouling, debris, erosion and survey burden. Kappel: blade tips curved to the suction side as an integrated winglet - weakens the tip vortex at the same diameter, no new appendage, smoother wake and less vibration, but modest, hull-specific, costly to design and hard to repair. Contra-rotating: two coaxial propellers turning opposite ways recovering swirl - highest theoretical gain, lower loading per propeller, torque cancelled, but complex shafting and gearing, concentric shaft sealing as the weak point, and limited service experience. Choose by thrust loading. Give no percentages.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the four ways a propeller loses energy, and what caps blade loading.
retrieval_cards.answer: Axial or slipstream loss - kinetic energy in the accelerated race. Rotational loss - swirl left in the race, the largest recoverable loss. Frictional loss - viscous drag on the blades. Tip vortex loss - pressure equalising around the tip. Cavitation caps how hard a blade may be loaded, through erosion, vibration and noise.

retrieval_cards.prompt: When does a duct make a ship worse, and why?
retrieval_cards.answer: At light thrust loading and higher speed. The duct is an appendage with its own drag; the accelerating effect and the duct's own thrust only outweigh that drag when the propeller is heavily loaded, as on a tug, trawler or slow full-form ship. On a fast, lightly loaded ship the drag dominates and efficiency falls.
retrieval_cards.why: The central discriminating fact about ducted propellers.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a Kappel propeller and what does it attack?
retrieval_cards.answer: A conventional-diameter propeller whose blade tips are curved smoothly towards the suction side as an integrated, continuous winglet - not a bolted-on end plate. It redistributes load outboard while weakening and displacing the tip vortex, so it attacks tip vortex loss at the same diameter, and gives a smoother wake into the rudder with lower pressure pulses.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates routinely describe it as an add-on device, which it is not.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does a contra-rotating arrangement recover, and what is its main practical weakness?
retrieval_cards.answer: It recovers the rotational energy - swirl - left in the race by the forward propeller, which is the largest single recoverable loss in a conventional installation. Its main practical weakness is mechanical: coaxial inner and outer shafting with complex gearing, and the sealing of two concentric shafts at the stern tube, which is the recognised reliability weak point. Maintenance, alignment and dry-dock withdrawal are all harder.
retrieval_cards.why: The theory is attractive; the objection is engineering, and that is what is examined.

blocks.h: 1. The instrument, and which revision applies

blocks.p: The question names MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3. The circular was originally approved jointly by the Facilitation Committee and the Maritime Safety Committee in 2017, superseding the interim guidelines in MSC.1/Circ.1526. The edition in force at this examination is Rev.3, dated 4 April 2025, approved by the Maritime Safety Committee at its 108th session (15 to 24 May 2024) and the Facilitation Committee at its forty-ninth session (10 to 14 March 2025). Name the revision you are answering on - this circular has been revised three times and the content of three of the four limbs below depends on which edition you mean.

The Guidelines define maritime cyber risk as a measure of the extent to which a technology asset is threatened by a potential circumstance or event, which may result in shipping-related operational, safety or security failures as a consequence of information or systems being corrupted, lost or compromised (annex 1.1). Note the breadth: corrupted, lost or compromised - loss of availability counts, so a failure with no attacker at all is still a cyber risk.

Rev.3 also introduces the organising term used throughout the current text: a Computer Based System (CBS) is a programmable electronic device, or interoperable set of programmable electronic devices, and CBSs on board include both IT and OT systems. The Guidelines remain expressly recommendatory; section 7 below explains why that does not make them optional.

blocks.h: 2. The onboard systems exposed to cyber risk

blocks.p: Annex 2.2.1 makes the point the question is quoting: cyber-technologies are essential to systems critical to safety, security and protection of the marine environment, but the vulnerabilities created by accessing, interconnecting or networking these systems create cyber risks. The Guidelines say vulnerable systems could include, but are not limited to - so this is a floor, not a closed list. Under Rev.3 there are nine categories:

ul: Bridge systems - and Rev.3 spells out the examples: navigation systems, ship safety systems and communications systems. ECDIS, radar and ARPA, GNSS receivers, AIS, VDR, the integrated navigation system and the autopilot all sit here.

Cargo, bunkering, lubrication, ballast and other pumping handling and management systems - loading computers and stability software, tanker cargo control, container and reefer monitoring, level and valve control, and the ballast water management system.

Propulsion, fuel and machinery management and power control systems - main engine and auxiliary control, the alarm and monitoring system, the power management system, fuel-changeover control and remote OEM diagnostics.
Security, access control and surveillance systems - ship security alarm arrangements, CCTV, electronic door and gangway control.
Passenger and crew servicing and management systems - boarding, embarkation and property management systems holding personal and payment data for passengers and crew.

Passenger, crew and subcontracted service personnel facing public networks - passenger and crew Wi-Fi and entertainment, which are exposed by design, and the networks offered to riding squads and service technicians.
Administrative and crew welfare systems - the ship business network, planned maintenance and procurement, and crew internet.
Ship-port interfaces - the systems through which the ship exchanges data with the terminal and the port community.
Ship-to-shore integrated systems - for example remote control systems and Maritime Autonomous Surface Ship arrangements, where a shore station participates directly in controlling the ship.

blocks.p: One structural point is worth a line: the last two heads, ship-port interfaces and ship-to-shore integrated systems, extend the boundary of the problem beyond the ship's own hull, which is the direction the whole subject is moving.

blocks.h: 3. What cyber risk management means, and where it starts

blocks.p: Annex 3.1 defines cyber risk management as the process of identifying, analysing, assessing, and communicating a cyber-related risk and accepting, avoiding, transferring or mitigating it to an acceptable level, considering costs and benefits of actions taken to stakeholders. Two halves: assess the risk, then take one of four decisions about it. The goal (3.2) is to support safe and secure shipping that is operationally resilient to cyber risks - resilience, not immunity.

Annex 3.3 places the starting point: effective cyber risk management should start at the senior management level, which should embed a culture of cyber risk awareness into all levels of the organization and ensure a regime that is holistic and flexible, in continuous operation and constantly evaluated through effective feedback mechanisms. Annex 3.4 gives the accepted method: compare the organization's current and desired postures, and address the gaps through a prioritized cyber risk management plan, so resources go where the risk is.

Annex 3.5 sets out six functional elements, and states that they are not sequential - all should be concurrent and continuous in practice and incorporated appropriately in a risk management framework. Rev.3 adds that the controls listed under each element are the minimum controls, and more may be required depending on the risk evaluation:

ul: GOVERN - establish and monitor the organization's cyber risk management strategy, expectations and policies; define personnel roles and responsibilities for cyber risk management; and ensure business continuity, such as backup management and disaster recovery, and crisis management.
Identify - determine the current cyber risk to ships and to ship/port interfaces, and identify the systems, assets, data and capabilities that, when disrupted, pose risks to ship operations.
Protect - implement risk control processes and measures to protect Computer Based Systems, together with contingency planning, so that shipping operations continue.
Detect - develop, implement and practise the activities necessary to detect a cyber-event in a timely manner.
Respond - develop, implement and practise activities and plans to provide resilience and to restore systems necessary for shipping operations or services impaired by a cyber-event.
Recover - identify and implement measures to restore onboard Computer Based Systems impacted by a cyber-event.

blocks.p: Govern is the element that is easiest to under-answer, and it is now first. It carries two named sub-controls: designate a person or entity accountable for the planning, resourcing and execution of cybersecurity activities, and ensure that person or entity has the necessary authority and support, and sufficient knowledge and expertise in cyber risk management. In other words the circular now asks, in terms, who owns this and can they actually do it - which is a management question rather than a technical one and belongs in an Engineering Management answer.

Note also the verb that Rev.3 repeats: practise. Detect and Respond both require the activities to be practised, not merely written. Annex 3.6 adds that together the elements constitute an ongoing process with effective feedback mechanisms, and 3.7 that awareness must be appropriate to each person's role. Writing the elements out as a six-step sequence to be worked through once is the commonest error on this limb.

blocks.h: 5. Why cyber security matters in the maritime sector

blocks.p: The Guidelines give the reason directly: risk management has traditionally been focused on the physical domain, and greater reliance on digitization, integration, automation and network-based systems has created an increasing need for cyber risk management in shipping. Five features make the shipping case distinct:

ul: A compromise becomes a safety event. Annex 2.2.5 says so - where vulnerabilities are exposed there are implications for the confidentiality, integrity and availability of data and for the safety and security of the ship, particularly where bridge navigation, main propulsion or cargo on/off-loading systems are compromised. Grounding, collision, loss of propulsion and pollution are cyber outcomes, not merely data outcomes.

IT and OT are connected, so an office problem becomes an engine-room problem. The mechanism is inappropriate connection between the two, or a procedural lapse such as the inappropriate use of removable media.
The threat need not be malicious. Software maintenance and user permissions sit alongside hacking and malware as sources of cyber risk.

The exposure runs down the supply chain. Annex 2.2.6 requires effective management to consider third-party vendors, embedded systems, and the software and hardware supply chains, and the maintenance devices brought aboard to service CBSs - the service laptop is itself an attack path.

The ship is hard to defend. Inadequacies in design, integration and maintenance and lapses in cyberdiscipline - weak passwords, absence of network segregation. Mixed-vendor equipment on long lifecycles, a small rotating crew and a constrained satellite link make patching, monitoring and specialist support all harder than ashore.

blocks.p: The management conclusion the Guidelines draw is that technologies and threats change too quickly to be addressed only through technical standards - which is why the answer is a risk-management regime placed inside existing safety and security management practice rather than beside it.
Rev.3 promotes both to formal definitions at annex 2.1, and supplies its own examples - which the limb expressly asks for:

Information Technology (IT) - CBSs focused on the use of data as information, including software, hardware and communication technologies, for example commercial information, or data about the crew such as salaries and certificates. Operational Technology (OT) - CBSs focused on the use of data to control or monitor physical processes, for example the main engine's oil temperature levels, which are forwarded to the control room.
