questions.short_title: Main Engine Failure to Respond to Bridge Control
questions.text_verbatim: Whilst approaching dock gates, the main engines did not respond to bridge control, driving ahead instead of braking astern, until the bow made contact with the dock wall. As Chief Engineer, report to head office why the engines failed to respond to Bridge control, the temporary measure instituted to avoid further trouble on this voyage and suggesting permanent measures to avoid repetition in the future.
decomposition: The report itself - form, addressee, and the evidence to be preserved and attached
Immediate action taken and the condition of the ship after contact
Why the engines did not respond - the control chain, fault by fault
The distinction the report must draw: lost control, incapable engine, or a late order
Temporary measures instituted for the remainder of this voyage
Permanent measures - technical
Permanent measures - management, testing and the statutory follow-up
reuse_evidence: VERIFIED DONOR: QP2403-Q8. Direct pair audit, ratio 1.0000 - EXACT. No wording delta. Neither sitting prints a mark allocation.

No blanket reset instruction was introduced and no SOLAS or ISM citation was manufactured to decorate an answer that does not need one.

The stem does not state the engine type, whether the installation is camshaft or electronically controlled, whether the control system is pneumatic or electronic, or whether a controllable pitch propeller is fitted. The answer therefore presents a FAULT TREE across the plausible architectures rather than a single diagnosis, and says so. That is the correct treatment of an under-specified scenario and is not a limitation of research.
The report format used is a conventional company incident report. No company procedure was available, and none is claimed.

blocks.h: 1. The report, and the evidence behind it

blocks.p: The report is addressed to the Designated Person and the technical superintendent, copied to the master, and headed with ship, voyage, port, berth, date and time and the bare fact - that on approaching the dock gates the main engine did not respond to bridge control, ran ahead when astern was ordered, and the bow made contact with the dock wall.

It is structured as summary; sequence of events; damage sustained; cause; temporary measures instituted; permanent measures recommended. Two disciplines matter more than the format. Separate fact from opinion, and label the opinion as opinion - this report will be read by the classification society, by underwriters and quite possibly by an investigating authority, and a confident wrong diagnosis in the first report is very difficult to withdraw. And preserve the evidence before anything is reset or repaired.

Attached: the engine movement and telegraph logger record, the alarm and monitoring history, the control system fault log downloaded rather than cleared, the VDR data secured before it is overwritten, the bell book and engine room log, and the maintenance and test records for the remote control, control air and starting air systems, including the date of the last proven astern test.

blocks.h: 2. Immediate action and the state of the ship

ul: Control was taken at the local manoeuvring platform, the engine stopped and astern movement obtained locally; the master was informed immediately and the bridge advised to call for tug assistance.

After contact: forepeak, forward tanks and void spaces sounded, and an internal inspection made for set-in plating, fractured or cracked welds, and ingress. Forward draught, list and trim checked for change.
Pollution risk assessed - whether any bunker or oily tank lies in the affected area, and whether any boundary is compromised.
Machinery secured and not restarted on bridge control; the engine left available on local control only.

Notifications made to company, classification society, flag State and the port authority as the circumstances required, and the occurrence recorded as a reportable event under the safety management system.

blocks.h: 3. Why the engines did not respond

blocks.p: The bridge control chain runs: bridge lever and telegraph → control transmitter → remote control system → safety and interlock logic → control air → starting air distributor and manoeuvring valves → reversing arrangement → fuel. A failure anywhere in that chain produces the same symptom on the bridge, which is why the report must work through it systematically rather than name a favourite cause.

ul: Control signal. Bridge lever encoder or potentiometer fault; chafed, broken or water-ingressed control cable; loose terminal; failed input/output card; loss of control system power or a failed UPS battery that had never been load-tested.

Control logic and location. Control not correctly transferred to the bridge, or a take-over left in an intermediate state; a mismatch between lever position and actual demand; loss of shaft speed or direction feedback, so the system never confirmed the reversal and held the ahead order.

Control air. On pneumatic and hybrid systems this is the classic cause of an intermittent failure: low control air pressure, moisture, oil carry-over or ice in the lines, a sticking pilot valve, a leaking diaphragm, a blocked orifice, a dirty filter or reducing valve, or water carried over from an undrained receiver.

Starting air. Receiver pressure fallen after repeated manoeuvres; starting air distributor timing or leakage; a stuck cylinder starting valve; the main starting valve failing to open; line drains left shut.

Reversing arrangement. On a camshaft engine, low servo oil pressure or a sticking reversing servo so the camshaft failed to shift, worn linkage, or a reversing interlock never satisfied so fuel was never admitted in the astern direction. On an electronically controlled engine, an ECU or hydraulic control unit fault, or an angle encoder failure, with a latched alarm blocking the reversal.
Fuel side. A sticking fuel rack or index linkage, so the engine received the order but no fuel.

Interlocks and safety system. Turning gear interlock, a low lubricating oil pressure or other shutdown active, an unacknowledged alarm inhibiting a start - or, worse, an override left in place from earlier work.

Human and organisational. This must be stated honestly: the astern movement may have been ordered too late for the engine to absorb the headway, or the astern power may have been insufficient for the displacement and approach speed. It is also relevant whether a full astern trial was carried out before arrival and, if not, why not.

blocks.p: The most probable composite explanation, and the one the report should advance as a working hypothesis until proven, is a latent defect in the remote control or control air system which only manifested under the rapid, repeated manoeuvring of a dock approach, on a system whose astern function had not recently been proven under load. No protective trip should be reset, and no interlock bypassed, before the cause is established - resetting destroys the evidence and may re-create the hazard.

blocks.h: 4. Lost control, incapable engine, or a late order

blocks.p: The report must distinguish three genuinely different failures, because the temporary and permanent measures differ completely and an incorrect classification sends the company down the wrong corrective path.

ul: Loss of remote (bridge) control. The engine was capable of running astern but never received or executed the order. The remedy is immediate transfer to the engine control room or local station - which is precisely why those independent control positions are required - and then repair of the control system.

Mechanical inability to produce astern thrust. The engine could not start or run astern at all: starting air, reversing arrangement, or fuel. Transferring control would have achieved nothing; the remedy is mechanical.

An adequate response ordered too late. The engine did respond, but the headway could not be absorbed in the distance available. The remedy is navigational and procedural - notice of engines, approach speed, tug use - not engineering.

blocks.p: The engine movement recorder settles it: it shows what was ordered on the bridge, at what time, whether the engine received the order, and whether and when the shaft actually reversed. Until that record has been read, the report should attribute cause to neither the bridge nor the engine room. Saying so explicitly is a mark of a competent report rather than a defensive one.

blocks.h: 5. Temporary measures for the remainder of the voyage

blocks.p: These were instituted immediately and are recorded as risk controls, not repairs.

ul: All manoeuvring from the engine control room or local platform until the cause is proven and rectified, with a qualified engineer stationed at the manoeuvring platform for every arrival, departure and passage in confined waters.
Two independent, tested means of communication between bridge and engine room, with an agreed and rehearsed order-and-repeat protocol, and the engine movement book kept manually.
A full ahead and astern engine trial before every arrival, conducted at a safe distance from danger and recorded - the astern movement in particular, which is the function that failed.
Control air system: receivers and lines drained, filters renewed or dried, reducing valves checked, air dryer proved, and control air pressure and quality confirmed before each manoeuvring period.
Starting air: both receivers at full pressure before manoeuvring, compressors confirmed on automatic, and all drains proved clear.
Increased notice of engines, earlier stand-by, and a reduced approach speed; tug assistance for berthing and unberthing for the remainder of the voyage.
The master to brief pilots and port authorities of the restriction, and to consider daylight-only berthing.
No undocumented overrides, and no bypass or isolation without the agreement of class.
A written risk assessment and a toolbox talk with the engine room and bridge teams; class notified and attendance arranged at the next convenient port.

Root cause analysis with the maker's service engineer and with class in attendance, working from the downloaded fault log rather than from a cleared system. Repair or renew the proven defective component, not the suspected one.
If the control system is obsolete or no longer supported, plan a controlled upgrade or retrofit with assured spares support, rather than repeated repair of unobtainable parts.

Control air quality. Fit or renew a refrigerant or desiccant dryer and coalescing filters, fit automatic drains, use corrosion-resistant piping, and introduce periodic dew point checks. Fit a low control air pressure alarm if not already provided.

Verify genuine redundancy. Confirm that the bridge, engine control room and local positions are truly independent, with separate power supplies and a UPS with a tested battery and a defined replacement interval. Establish that no single point of failure is common to all three - which is the design question this incident raises.
Critical spares. Hold control cards, solenoid and pilot valves, pressure switches and position sensors on board as identified critical spares.

Fit independent shaft speed and direction of rotation indication on the bridge if it is not already provided, so that the bridge team can see whether the engine has actually reversed rather than inferring it from the telegraph.

Report and analyse the occurrence under the safety management system, with corrective action assigned, dated and verified. A propulsion failure resulting in contact damage is exactly the kind of hazardous occurrence the system exists to capture.

Identify the remote control system and the control air system as critical equipment. Critical equipment attracts specific measures to promote reliability, including regular testing of arrangements that are not in continuous use - and the astern function under bridge control is precisely such an arrangement.

Planned maintenance. Bring the remote control system, control air system, starting air distributor, reversing servo and interlock logic into the PMS with defined intervals and, critically, functional tests rather than visual inspections. A test that does not prove the astern function does not test what failed.

Contingency procedure. Write a documented loss of bridge control procedure into the SMS - who takes control, where, how the order is passed and acknowledged, and what the bridge does meanwhile - and drill it jointly with the bridge team, not as an engine room exercise.

Checklists. Amend the pre-arrival and manoeuvring checklists to require a recorded ahead and astern engine test at a stated time before arrival, and include propulsion status and any restriction in the master and pilot exchange.

Precursors. Review earlier logs and defect reports for intermittent faults on the same system, and state in the report whether any existed and, if so, why they were not escalated. If the answer is uncomfortable, that is the most valuable finding in the document.

Fleet action. Check sister ships and similar installations across the fleet, and review the company PMS templates. Close the loop by verifying effectiveness at the next internal audit rather than closing the non-conformity on the strength of the repair alone.

blocks.p: The stem is a single paragraph but it contains three explicit demands: why the engines failed, the temporary measure instituted to avoid further trouble on this voyage, and permanent measures to avoid repetition. Roughly a third of the marks each. The commonest failure is to write four hundred words of fault-finding and then two lines on permanent measures, throwing away a third of the question.

The second structural decision is route step 4. Separating loss of remote control from mechanical inability to go astern from a late order is what turns a list of possible faults into an engineer's analysis - and the examiner is looking for exactly that judgement, because the three lead to entirely different corrective action.

blocks.h: Answer it as a report, because it says so

blocks.p: The stem says "As Chief Engineer, report to head office". Use report form: a heading, short numbered sections, and factual language. Two things earn credit almost free - separating fact from opinion, and listing the attachments (movement recorder, alarm history, fault log, VDR, bell book, logs, maintenance records). They show you understand who will read the document and what it will be used for.
Do not use the report to allocate blame. A first report that blames the bridge, or the engine room, before the movement recorder has been read is a report that will have to be withdrawn.

blocks.h: The safety point that must not be got wrong

blocks.p: Never reset protective trips or bypass interlocks to get the engine running again before the cause is known. A trip that operated may have been doing its job; an interlock that blocked the reversal may have been protecting the engine. Resetting also destroys the evidence in the fault log. If an isolation or bypass is unavoidable to move the ship, it must be risk-assessed, documented, time-limited and agreed with class - never done quietly.

ul: Writing only about the engine and ignoring the control system, which is where this fault almost certainly lay.
Giving one cause confidently. The scenario does not state the engine or control architecture; a fault tree is the correct answer, and saying why is a strength.
Skipping temporary measures, which are a third of the marks and the part that shows operational judgement.
Recommending "repair the fault" as the permanent measure. The permanent measure is the system change that stops it recurring - testing regime, air quality, redundancy, PMS, critical spares.
Forgetting the ship. After contact with a dock wall, soundings, internal inspection and pollution assessment come before diagnosis.
Blaming the bridge team. It may be right, but not before the record is read.
Recommending resetting trips to prove the engine works.
Loss of control is not inability to go astern. The single most valuable distinction in the answer.
Control air moisture. The classic cause of an intermittent failure that appears only under repeated manoeuvring - and a favourite oral question.
Repeated manoeuvring depletes starting air. A dock approach is exactly when receiver pressure falls and the distributor is worked hardest.
The astern function is rarely tested. Ahead running proves itself every day; astern is proved only when it is deliberately tested, which is why it is the function that fails when needed.
Critical equipment. Naming the remote control and control air systems as critical equipment, requiring regular testing of arrangements not in continuous use, is the management-level answer.
Precursors. Asking whether the fault had been seen before, and whether it was escalated, is what distinguishes a management-level report.
"The engine will not answer the bridge. What do you do first?" - take local control, get the engine responding from the platform, tell the bridge, and get tugs. Diagnose second.
"How would you know whether the bridge ordered astern?" - the engine movement and telegraph logger, and the VDR.

"Why does control air moisture cause an intermittent fault?" - water and oil collect in low points and pilot valves, and a valve that works in steady conditions sticks under rapid repeated operation, or ice forms on expansion.
"Would you reset the trip to get moving?" - no, not before the cause is known; and any unavoidable bypass must be risk-assessed, documented, time-limited and agreed with class.

"What is your permanent recommendation in one sentence?" - a proven astern test before every arrival, control air drying and filtration, verified redundancy with separate supplies, and both systems identified as critical equipment in the PMS.
"What do you check on the ship after contact?" - forepeak and forward tank soundings, internal structural inspection, draughts and trim, and pollution risk.

blocks.p: The report has three demands - WHY, NOW, NEVER AGAIN. For WHY, walk the chain in order: LEVER, SIGNAL, LOGIC, AIR, START, REVERSE, FUEL, INTERLOCK. For NOW, three words: LOCAL, TEST, TUGS - manoeuvre from local control, prove astern before every arrival, take tugs. For NEVER AGAIN, four words: CAUSE, AIR, REDUNDANCY, TESTING.
This is an operational question and no instrument is quoted. Two regimes frame the follow-up and are referred to at the level of their effect only:

ul: The ISM Code - the obligations to report and analyse non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences; to maintain the ship and equipment including the identification of critical equipment and systems whose sudden failure may create a hazardous situation, with specific measures to promote reliability including regular testing of arrangements not in continuous use; and emergency preparedness through drills.

SOLAS chapter II-1 - the requirement that propulsion machinery be controllable from the navigation bridge, with an independent local means of control and indication of shaft speed and direction of thrust. That architecture is exactly why the temporary measure in route step 5 is available.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the limits of this answer

blocks.p: The ISM Code and SOLAS chapter II-1 were not read in licensed consolidated editions this session. Both are therefore referred to at the level of their well-known effect, with no clause quoted and no regulation number asserted. This is the same posture already recorded for the ISM Code in Q5 of this paper, and no argument in the answer depends on precise wording.

The stem does not state the engine type, the control architecture, whether the installation is camshaft or electronically controlled, or whether a controllable pitch propeller is fitted. The answer therefore presents a fault tree across the plausible architectures and says so. That is the correct treatment of an under-specified scenario, not a gap in research - and in the examination, stating that the diagnosis depends on the installation is itself a mark of competence.
The report format used is a conventional company incident report. No company procedure was available and none is claimed.

This is a Chief Engineer operational and diagnostic scenario. No instrument prescribes the sequence, the donor carries an empty regulations list, and that was RETAINED - no SOLAS or ISM citation was manufactured to decorate an answer that does not need one.

The safe diagnostic sequence is unchanged between the sittings: bridge and engine-room communication, transfer of control, permissives and interlocks, starting air, fuel and control system, local control, mechanical readiness, controlled restoration and test, then record and root cause.

No blanket reset or bypass instruction was introduced. The donor's discipline that no protective trip is reset and no interlock bypassed before the cause is established is carried unchanged, because resetting destroys evidence and may re-create the hazard.

steps.title: The report, and the evidence behind it
points: address it to the Designated Person and technical superintendent, copied to the master
head it with ship, voyage, port, date and time, and the fact of contact
structure: summary, sequence, damage, cause, temporary measures, permanent measures
separate FACT from OPINION and label the opinion as such
the report will be read by class, underwriters and possibly investigators
preserve and attach the engine movement and telegraph logger record
attach the alarm and monitoring history, the control system fault log and the VDR data
attach bell book, engine room log, and the maintenance and test records for the control system
preserve the evidence BEFORE anything is reset or repaired

steps.title: Immediate action and the state of the ship
points: control taken locally and the engine stopped, then astern from the manoeuvring platform
master informed, tugs and the port informed, general alarm as the situation required
after contact: sound forepeak, forward tanks and void spaces
internal inspection for set-in plating, fractured welds and ingress
check bow structure, forward draught and any list or trim change
assess pollution risk and any bunker tank in the affected area
no engine restart on bridge control until the cause is understood
notify company, class, flag State and the port authority as required

steps.title: Why the engines did not respond
points: the chain is: bridge lever, control transmitter, remote control system, interlocks, air, reversing, fuel
CONTROL SIGNAL - lever encoder or potentiometer fault, chafed cable, loose terminal, failed I/O card
CONTROL SIGNAL - loss of control system power or a failed UPS battery
CONTROL LOGIC - control not correctly transferred, or a take-over left in the wrong state
CONTROL LOGIC - loss of shaft speed or direction feedback, so reversal was never confirmed
PNEUMATIC - low control air pressure, moisture, oil or ice in the lines, sticking pilot valve
PNEUMATIC - blocked orifice, dirty filter or reducer, water carried over from the receiver
STARTING AIR - low receiver pressure after repeated manoeuvres, distributor timing, stuck starting valve
REVERSING - servo oil pressure low, camshaft failing to shift, worn linkage, interlock never satisfied
ELECTRONIC ENGINES - ECU or HCU fault, angle encoder failure, latched alarm blocking the reversal
FUEL - sticking fuel rack or index linkage so no fuel was admitted astern
INTERLOCKS - turning gear, low lube oil pressure, an unacknowledged shutdown, or an override left in place
HUMAN AND ORGANISATIONAL - astern ordered too late, or insufficient astern power for the headway
the likely composite: a latent fault that only appeared under repeated rapid manoeuvring

steps.title: Lost control, incapable engine, or a late order
points: these are THREE different failures with three different remedies - the report must say which
LOST REMOTE CONTROL - the engine could have run astern but never received or executed the order
the remedy is transfer to the engine control room or local station, which is why they exist
INCAPABLE ENGINE - it could not start or run astern: air, reversing gear or fuel
the remedy is mechanical repair; transferring control would have achieved nothing
LATE OR INADEQUATE ORDER - the engine did respond but the headway could not be absorbed
the remedy is navigational and procedural, not engineering
the movement recorder settles it - what was ordered, what was received, what the shaft did
do not blame the bridge or the engine before the record is read

steps.title: Temporary measures for the remainder of the voyage
points: ALL manoeuvring from the engine control room or local platform until the cause is proven
a qualified engineer stationed at the manoeuvring platform for every arrival and departure
two independent, tested means of bridge to engine room communication, with an agreed protocol
a full ahead and ASTERN engine trial before every arrival, at a safe distance, and recorded
control air: drain receivers and lines, renew or dry filters, prove pressure and quality
starting air: both receivers at full pressure before manoeuvring, drains proved clear
increased notice of engines, earlier stand-by, and a reduced approach speed
TUG ASSISTANCE for berthing and unberthing for the rest of the voyage
master to brief pilots and the port; consider daylight-only berthing
no undocumented overrides, and no bypass without class agreement
record a risk assessment and hold a toolbox talk; notify class and arrange attendance
state plainly in the report that these are MITIGATIONS, not repairs

steps.title: Permanent measures - technical
points: formal root cause analysis with the maker's service engineer and class in attendance
download and analyse the control system fault log rather than clearing it
renew or repair the proven defective component, not the suspected one
if the control system is obsolete and unsupported, plan a controlled upgrade
control air quality - fit or renew dryer and coalescing filters, automatic drains
periodic dew point checks and an alarm on low control air pressure
verify genuine redundancy - independent bridge, control room and local paths
separate power supplies and a tested UPS with a battery replacement interval
confirm there is no single point of failure common to all three control positions
hold control cards, solenoids, pilot valves and sensors as identified critical spares
fit independent shaft speed and direction indication on the bridge if not already fitted

steps.title: Permanent measures - management and follow-up
points: report and analyse the occurrence under the safety management system
identify the remote control and control air systems as CRITICAL EQUIPMENT
critical equipment requires specific measures to promote reliability, including regular testing
bring the remote control system, control air, starting air distributor, reversing servo and interlocks into the planned maintenance system
functional testing, not visual inspection - a test that proves the astern function
write a documented LOSS OF BRIDGE CONTROL contingency procedure into the SMS
drill it, jointly, bridge team and engine room
update the manoeuvring and pre-arrival checklists to require a recorded astern test
master and pilot exchange to include propulsion status and any restriction
check the earlier logs for precursor intermittent faults, and say in the report whether any existed
fleet-wide check of sister ships and a review of the company PMS
close the loop - verify effectiveness at the next internal audit

questions.understand_first: This is a management-level incident report, not a fault-finding exercise, and the stem tells you its three parts: WHY it failed, what you did NOW for the rest of this voyage, and what must change so it NEVER happens again. The engineering insight the examiner is looking for is a distinction: losing bridge control is not the same as the engine being unable to go astern, and neither is the same as an astern order given too late to stop the ship. Those three have three different remedies, and the engine movement recorder tells you which one you had. The safety line you must not cross is resetting trips or bypassing interlocks to get moving before you know the cause.
questions.memory_cue: Three demands - WHY, NOW, NEVER AGAIN. WHY walks the chain in route step 3: LEVER, SIGNAL, LOGIC, AIR, START, REVERSE, FUEL, INTERLOCK (3). NOW is three words in route step 5: LOCAL, TEST, TUGS (5). NEVER AGAIN is four words across route steps 6 and 7: CAUSE, AIR, REDUNDANCY, TESTING (6, 7).

quick_revision.recall_15s: Report to the Designated Person and superintendent: summary, sequence, damage, cause, temporary measures, permanent measures. Preserve the movement recorder, alarm history, control system fault log and VDR before resetting anything. Ship first - sound forepeak and forward tanks, inspect internally, check pollution risk. The chain is lever, signal, logic, control air, starting air, reversing, fuel, interlocks; control air moisture and an unproven astern function are the classic causes. Distinguish loss of remote control from mechanical inability to go astern from an astern order given too late - three different remedies, and the movement recorder decides which. Temporary: manoeuvre from local control with an engineer at the platform, two communication means, a recorded ahead and astern trial before every arrival, drained control and starting air, more notice of engines, and tugs. Permanent: root cause with maker and class, air drying and filtration, verified redundancy with separate supplies and tested UPS, both systems identified as critical equipment with functional testing in the PMS, critical spares, a documented loss-of-control procedure drilled jointly, and a fleet-wide check.
keywords: WHY, NOW, NEVER AGAIN - three demands
preserve evidence before resetting anything
lever, signal, logic, air, start, reverse, fuel, interlock
control air moisture - the classic intermittent fault
lost control is not inability to go astern
local control, recorded astern trial, tugs
critical equipment and regular testing of arrangements not in continuous use
never reset trips before the cause is known
critical_numbers: Three demands in the stem: cause, temporary measure, permanent measures
Three failure categories: lost remote control, incapable engine, late order
Three control positions: bridge, engine control room, local platform
Two independent means of bridge to engine room communication
One recorded ahead and astern engine trial before every arrival
quick_revision.critical_regulation: No instrument is quoted. Two regimes frame the follow-up at the level of their effect only: the ISM Code obligations to report and analyse hazardous occurrences and to identify CRITICAL EQUIPMENT with specific measures to promote reliability including regular testing of arrangements not in continuous use; and the SOLAS chapter II-1 architecture requiring bridge control of propulsion with an independent local means and indication of shaft speed and direction, which is what makes the temporary measure possible.
quick_revision.major_trap: Treating this as a fault-finding question and losing the two thirds of the marks that sit in the temporary and permanent measures. The second trap is failing to distinguish loss of remote control from mechanical inability to produce astern thrust from an astern order given too late - three different failures with three different remedies. The third is recommending that trips be reset to get the engine running before the cause is known.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the bridge control failure report.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 The report and its evidence. 2 Immediate action and the state of the ship. 3 Why the engines did not respond. 4 Lost control, incapable engine, or a late order. 5 Temporary measures for this voyage. 6 Permanent measures - technical. 7 Permanent measures - management and follow-up.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem has three demands; steps 5, 6 and 7 carry two thirds of the marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Walk the bridge control chain from lever to fuel.
retrieval_cards.answer: Bridge lever and telegraph, control transmitter, remote control system, safety and interlock logic, control air, starting air distributor and manoeuvring valves, reversing arrangement (camshaft servo or electronic control units), fuel index. A failure anywhere gives the same symptom on the bridge.
retrieval_cards.why: The systematic walk is what makes the diagnosis credible.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish the three failures this scenario could be, and how you tell them apart.
retrieval_cards.answer: Loss of remote control - the engine could run astern but never received or executed the order; remedy is local control then repair. Mechanical inability to produce astern thrust - air, reversing gear or fuel; transferring control achieves nothing and the remedy is mechanical. An adequate response ordered too late - the engine did respond but the headway could not be absorbed; the remedy is navigational and procedural. The engine movement recorder shows what was ordered, what was received and whether the shaft reversed.
retrieval_cards.why: The single most valuable judgement in the whole answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is control air moisture the classic cause of an intermittent bridge control failure?
retrieval_cards.answer: Water and oil collect at low points, in filters and in pilot valves. A valve that operates reliably in steady conditions sticks under rapid repeated operation, and ice can form where air expands. The fault therefore appears exactly when the system is worked hardest - a dock approach - and cannot be reproduced afterwards at the berth.
retrieval_cards.why: Explains why the fault appeared when it did and disappeared afterwards.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What temporary measures would you institute for the rest of the voyage?
retrieval_cards.answer: All manoeuvring from the engine control room or local platform with an engineer stationed there; two independent tested means of communication with an agreed protocol; a recorded ahead and astern engine trial at a safe distance before every arrival; control and starting air drained, filtered and proved; increased notice of engines and reduced approach speed; tug assistance for berthing; pilots and port informed; no undocumented overrides; class notified. These are mitigations, not repairs.
retrieval_cards.why: A third of the marks, and the part that shows operational judgement.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Would you reset the trip to get the engine running again?
retrieval_cards.answer: No - not before the cause is established. A trip that operated may have been doing its job and an interlock that blocked the reversal may have been protecting the engine; resetting also destroys the fault log evidence. If a bypass is unavoidable to move the ship it must be risk-assessed, documented, time-limited and agreed with class.
retrieval_cards.why: The safety judgement the examiner is most likely to probe.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the management-level permanent measure, expressed in safety-management terms?
retrieval_cards.answer: Identify the remote control system and the control air system as CRITICAL EQUIPMENT whose sudden operational failure may result in a hazardous situation, and apply specific measures to promote reliability - including regular functional testing of arrangements not in continuous use, which is exactly what the astern function is. Bring them into the planned maintenance system with functional tests rather than visual inspections.
retrieval_cards.why: Turns a repair into a system change, which is what "permanent measure" means.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What do you check on the ship immediately after contact with the dock wall?
retrieval_cards.answer: Sound the forepeak, forward tanks and void spaces; inspect internally for set-in plating, cracked or fractured welds and ingress; check forward draught, list and trim for change; assess pollution risk including any bunker or oily tank in the affected area; and notify company, class, flag State and port authority as required.
retrieval_cards.why: The ship comes before the diagnosis, and candidates routinely forget it.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: A management-level incident report with three explicit demands - cause, temporary measure for this voyage, permanent measures against repetition. The engineering discrimination being tested is between loss of remote control, mechanical inability to go astern, and an astern order given too late.

decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: Report form; a systematic walk of the control chain rather than a single guessed cause; the three-way distinction; and permanent measures that are SYSTEM changes rather than "repair the fault". A candidate who recommends resetting trips to restore propulsion has failed the safety test.

blocks.h: 1. What the Convention is, and how it is built

blocks.p: The Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 was adopted at the 94th (Maritime) Session of the International Labour Conference. It consolidated some sixty-eight earlier ILO maritime instruments into one, and is universally described as the fourth pillar of the international regulatory regime, standing beside SOLAS, MARPOL and STCW. It is often called the seafarers' bill of rights.

Its architecture is unusual and is worth a sentence in any answer. It has three parts: the Articles, which set out the general obligations; the Regulations; and the Code. Article VI then divides the Code in two - Part A contains Standards and is mandatory, while Part B contains Guidelines which are not mandatory but to which Members must give due consideration. Article VI.3 adds the flexibility mechanism of substantial equivalence: a Member may implement a Part A Standard differently provided the provision is substantially equivalent in achieving the general object and purpose.

The Regulations and Code are arranged in five Titles: Title 1 minimum requirements to work on a ship; Title 2 conditions of employment; Title 3 accommodation, recreational facilities, food and catering; Title 4 health protection, medical care, welfare and social security protection; and Title 5 compliance and enforcement. Article IV states the underlying rights: a safe and secure workplace, fair terms of employment, decent working and living conditions, and health protection, medical care, welfare measures and other forms of social protection.

The text in force at this sitting is the Convention as amended by the 2014, 2016, 2018 and 2022 amendments, approved at the 103rd, 105th, 107th and 110th Sessions of the Conference respectively. The 2022 set is the most recent in force, and it adds requirements in three of the five Titles, noted in their place below.

blocks.h: 2. Minimum requirements and the employment agreement

blocks.p: Title 1 controls who may go to sea.

ul: Minimum age (Reg 1.1). Standard A1.1.1 - the employment, engagement or work on board of any person under the age of 16 is prohibited. A1.1.2 - night work by seafarers under 18 is prohibited, "night" covering a period of at least nine hours starting no later than midnight and ending no earlier than 5 a.m. Hazardous work by those under 18 is likewise prohibited.

Medical fitness (Reg 1.2). A valid medical certificate is required before beginning work. Standard A1.2.7 - it is valid for a maximum of two years, or one year if the seafarer is under 18, and a certification of colour vision for a maximum of six years. An STCW medical certificate is accepted.

Training and recruitment (Regs 1.3 and 1.4). Seafarers must be trained and qualified for their duties, and recruitment and placement services must be regulated - notably, no fees are to be borne by the seafarer.

blocks.p: The seafarers' employment agreement (Reg 2.1) is the document the question names first. Standard A2.1.1 requires an agreement signed by both the seafarer and the shipowner or a representative, providing decent working and living conditions; the seafarer must be given an opportunity to examine it and to seek advice before signing, so that the agreement is freely entered into. Both parties hold a signed original, a copy is carried on board and available to the seafarer and to inspectors, and the seafarer receives a record of employment which contains no statement as to the quality of the work or the wages.

blocks.h: 3. Hours, wages, leave, repatriation and manning

blocks.p: Hours of work and rest (Reg 2.3) is the provision most tested in practice. Standard A2.3.3 sets the baseline at an eight-hour day with one day of rest per week and rest on public holidays. A2.3.5 then requires each Member to fix either a maximum number of hours of work or a minimum number of hours of rest:

ul: maximum hours of work - not exceeding 14 hours in any 24-hour period and 72 hours in any seven-day period; or
minimum hours of rest - not less than ten hours in any 24-hour period and 77 hours in any seven-day period.

blocks.p: Rest may be divided into no more than two periods, one of which must be at least six hours, with no more than fourteen hours between consecutive rest periods. A2.3.4 requires national standards to take account of the danger posed by fatigue, especially for those with navigational duties. A table of shipboard working arrangements is posted and records of daily hours are kept.

Wages (Reg 2.2) are paid at intervals no greater than monthly, with a monthly account and a means of transmitting allotments home. Leave (Reg 2.4) gives paid annual leave, and Reg 2.7 requires ships to be sufficiently and efficiently manned. Repatriation (Reg 2.5) is the seafarer's ultimate protection: Standard A2.5.1 gives entitlement when the agreement expires while abroad, when it is terminated by the shipowner or by the seafarer for justified reasons, and when the seafarer can no longer carry out the duties. A2.5.2(b) requires the maximum service period on board after which repatriation falls due to be less than twelve months. The shipowner must also maintain financial security for abandonment, evidenced by a certificate carried on board, and a seafarer's wages continue during captivity following piracy or armed robbery.

blocks.h: 4. Accommodation, catering, health, welfare and social security

ul: Accommodation and recreational facilities (Reg 3.1). Accommodation must be safe and decent, with detailed requirements for size, headroom, heating, ventilation, lighting, sanitary facilities and hospital accommodation. Note the application rule: the construction standards apply only to ships built on or after the Convention entered into force for that Member. Accommodation is inspected on board at frequent, recorded intervals. Standard A3.1 paragraph 17 requires appropriate recreational facilities, amenities and services including SOCIAL CONNECTIVITY, adapted to meet the special needs of seafarers who must live and work on ships - the associated guidance addressing internet access at reasonable charges. Connectivity is a welfare requirement of the Convention, not a commercial courtesy.

Food and catering (Reg 3.2). Food and drinking water of appropriate quality, nutritional value and quantity, supplied free of charge during the period of engagement; ships' cooks must be trained and qualified, and no seafarer under 18 may serve as ship's cook.

Medical care (Reg 4.1). Health protection and medical care comparable to that available ashore, provided free of charge, including the right to visit a qualified doctor or dentist without delay in ports of call, where practicable, a medicine chest and medical guide, and access to radio or satellite medical advice.

Shipowners' liability (Reg 4.2). The shipowner bears the cost of sickness and injury occurring in service, and must hold financial security for contractual claims arising from death or long-term disability. Appendix A4-I lists the particulars the certificate must carry, and paragraph (g) now requires the name of the shipowner or of the REGISTERED OWNER where different from the shipowner - a direct response to layered ownership defeating claims.

Health and safety (Reg 4.3). Occupational safety and health policies and programmes, risk assessment and accident reporting, and - Standard A4.3.2 - a ship's safety committee where there are five or more seafarers. Harassment and bullying are expressly addressed in the guidance. Three further requirements matter to an engineer: Standard A4.3.1(b) requires the provision of all necessary APPROPRIATELY-SIZED personal protective equipment - equipment that does not fit is not compliance; Standard A4.3.2 read with Guideline B4.3.1.3 establishes the hierarchy of controls, requiring account to be taken of engineering and design control, and substitution of processes and procedures, which have precedence over personal protective equipment; and Standard A4.3.5(a) requires the flag State to ensure that all deaths of seafarers on its ships are adequately investigated and recorded, and reported annually to the Director-General of the International Labour Office for publication in a GLOBAL REGISTER.

Welfare and social security (Regs 4.4 and 4.5). Access to shore-based welfare facilities, and social security protection which, on ratification, must cover at least three of the nine branches listed in Standard A4.5.

blocks.h: 5. Flag State enforcement - certification and inspection

blocks.p: Title 5 is what makes the MLC enforceable rather than aspirational, and limb (b) cannot be answered without it.

The flag State certifies. Standard A5.1.3.1 - the maritime labour certificate is issued by the competent authority, or by a recognized organization duly authorized under Reg 5.1.2, for a period not exceeding five years, and is subject under A5.1.3.2 to an intermediate inspection between the second and third anniversary dates. It is accompanied by the Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance: Part I, drawn by the competent authority, listing the national requirements; and Part II, drawn by the shipowner, setting out the measures adopted to ensure ongoing compliance between inspections.

Appendix A5-I lists the working and living conditions that must be inspected and approved before certification. There are sixteen - minimum age, medical certification, qualifications, seafarers' employment agreements, use of licensed recruitment services, hours of work or rest, manning levels, accommodation, on-board recreational facilities, food and catering, health and safety and accident prevention, on-board medical care, on-board complaint procedures, payment of wages, financial security for repatriation and financial security relating to shipowners' liability. The last two were added by the 2014 amendments, which is why the list is sixteen and not the original fourteen. Beyond certification, Reg 5.1.4 requires a system of inspection and enforcement, Reg 5.1.5 requires on-board complaint procedures with safeguards against victimization and the right to complain directly to the master and to external authorities, and Reg 5.1.6 requires an official inquiry into any serious marine casualty.

blocks.h: 6. Port State control and the labour-supplying State

blocks.p: Under Regulation 5.2.1 an authorized officer in a port of another Member may inspect. The certificate and DMLC are accepted as prima facie evidence of compliance, and the inspection normally stops there. Standard A5.2.1.1 gives four triggers for a more detailed inspection:

ul: the required documents are not produced or maintained, are falsely maintained, lack the required information or are otherwise invalid;
there are clear grounds for believing that working and living conditions do not conform to the Convention;
there are reasonable grounds to believe the ship has changed flag to avoid compliance; or
there is a complaint alleging that specific conditions do not conform.

blocks.p: Appendix A5-III sets out the sixteen general areas open to such a detailed inspection - the same list as Appendix A5-I. Where conditions are clearly hazardous to safety, health or security, or the breach is serious or repeated, the ship may be detained until deficiencies are rectified. Article V.7 supplies the principle that makes this work commercially: ships flying the flag of a State that has not ratified must not receive more favourable treatment than those of a ratifying State. Two further limbs complete the architecture - Reg 5.2.2, which requires onshore seafarer complaint-handling procedures, and Reg 5.3, which places responsibilities on labour-supplying States such as India for recruitment, placement and social protection of their seafarers.
The Convention's weaknesses are structural rather than textual, and limb (b) is asking you to name them.

ul: Flag State capacity and delegation. Certification is almost universally delegated to recognized organizations under Reg 5.1.2, and the recognized organization is paid by the shipowner it inspects. Administrations with large registers and small staffs rely on that delegation entirely, so the quality of enforcement varies with the register rather than with the Convention.

Documentary compliance. Because the certificate and DMLC are prima facie evidence, a ship whose paperwork is in order will normally pass. The gap between a compliant file and a compliant ship is the central practical limitation.

Hours-of-rest records. The single most reported area of non-compliance, and structurally so: the record is generated by the person whose hours it records, under commercial pressure, on a ship manned to the minimum safe manning document. Port turnarounds, inspections and drills are absorbed by the crew and disappear from the record.

Uneven national implementation. Article VI.3 substantial equivalence and the non-mandatory status of Part B mean two ratifying States may impose materially different requirements. Seafarers of the same rank on the same trade can hold quite different entitlements.

The limits of port State control. An MLC inspection competes with SOLAS and MARPOL priorities during a short port stay; assessing wages, contracts and rest hours is a different skill from assessing equipment; and risk-based targeting under the regional memoranda means some ships are rarely inspected.

Who actually bears the sanction. Enforcement acts on the ship, through detention and delay. It does not reach the beneficial owner directly, and single-ship companies and layered ownership limit what a seafarer can recover. The financial security amendments were a direct response to exactly this problem in abandonment cases, and the requirement that the certificate now name the registered owner where different from the shipowner attacks the same weakness one layer further in.

Under-use of complaint procedures. Reg 5.1.5 gives the right and forbids victimization, but seafarers on short contracts in a competitive market fear blacklisting, so complaints are made late, ashore, or not at all.

Social security. Reg 4.5 is the weakest Title in practice: only three of nine branches are required at ratification, and portability between flag, nationality and manning-agent jurisdictions remains unresolved.

The absence of data - now being addressed. A recurring criticism has been that no one knows the true scale of seafarer death and injury, because reporting was fragmented across flags. Standard A4.3.5(a) now requires deaths to be investigated, recorded and reported annually to the ILO Director-General for a global register. It is a partial answer to the enforcement-data gap rather than a complete one - it measures the outcome rather than compelling the conditions - but it is the first Convention-level mechanism for counting.

External shocks. The COVID-19 crew change crisis demonstrated the ceiling: when States closed borders, seafarers served far beyond the repatriation limits and neither flag nor port States could give effect to Reg 2.5, notwithstanding repeated ILO and IMO appeals.

blocks.p: The marks are 8 + 8, and the two limbs are very different tasks. Limb (a) is coverage: the examiner has named five areas - employment contracts, working hours, accommodation, health and safety, medical care and welfare - and expects each to be reached. Route steps 2, 3 and 4 walk the Titles in order so that none is missed, which is the commonest way marks are lost here.

Limb (b) is evaluation, and it is the harder half. It names three targets - flag State jurisdiction, port State control, and non-compliance by shipowners and operators - so an answer that merely describes Title 5 has answered the wrong question. Steps 5 and 6 establish the machinery briefly because you cannot criticise what you have not described; step 7 is where the marks are.

blocks.h: THE TEMPORAL POINT - the 2022 amendments ARE in force, the 2025 amendments are NOT

blocks.p: This question is dated at both ends, and both ends can catch you.

The 2022 amendments entered into force on 23 December 2024 - ten months before this sitting - and are simply the law here. They were approved at the 110th Session of the International Labour Conference in June 2022, and the operative consolidation at this examination is the Convention as amended in 2014, 2016, 2018 and 2022. An answer written from older notes will be short by five requirements, four of which fall squarely in Title 3 and Title 4 that the examiner has expressly named.

The 2025 amendments, adopted at the 113th Session in June 2025, are NOT in force and must not appear. They were adopted four months before this sitting, which makes them unusually dangerous: material published in the second half of 2025 and afterwards will describe them in the present tense, and current ILO pages fold them into "the MLC as amended". They are expected to take effect in 2027. Adoption is not entry into force. If you mention them at all, mention them as a future development and say so.

blocks.h: The five 2022 requirements, and where each belongs

blocks.p: These are worth learning individually, because each attaches to a Standard the examiner has already asked about - they are not a separate topic:

ul: Social connectivity - Standard A3.1 paragraph 17. Recreational facilities, amenities and services must now include social connectivity, with the associated guidance addressing internet access at reasonable charges. This sits in Title 3, which limb (a) names. Connectivity is a welfare entitlement, not a perk.

Appropriately-sized PPE - Standard A4.3 paragraph 1(b). The precaution now expressly extends to providing all necessary appropriately-sized personal protective equipment. The word does real work: PPE issued in one size, which does not fit a substantial part of the crew, is not compliance.

The hierarchy of controls - Guideline B4.3.1 paragraph 3, with Standard A4.3 paragraph 2. Engineering and design control, and substitution of the dangerous by the less dangerous, have precedence over personal protective equipment. This is the standard occupational-hygiene hierarchy, now express in the Convention, and it is the most examinable of the five for an Engineering Management paper - it is a design and management duty, not a stores duty.

Deaths reported for a global register - Standard A4.3 paragraph 5(a). The flag State must ensure all seafarer deaths on its ships are adequately investigated and recorded, and reported annually to the Director-General of the ILO to be published in a global register. Use this twice: once in limb (a) as a flag-State duty, and once in limb (b), because it is a partial answer to the criticism that no one counts.

Registered owner on the financial security certificate - Appendix A4-I(g). The certificate must name the shipowner or the registered owner if different. It attacks layered ownership, which is one of limb (b)'s own complaints.

blocks.p: What did NOT change is the larger part of the answer, and it is worth knowing that too: the whole architecture of Articles, Regulations and Code, the five Titles, the hours limits, repatriation, the certificate and DMLC, the four PSC triggers, Article V.7, and the entire structural critique in limb (b). The route is identical to the March 2024 route; the content of two sections inside it grew.

blocks.h: A dating marker, and its limits

blocks.p: Appendix A5-I lists sixteen items, not the original fourteen - the two extra being the financial security items added in 2014. An answer that says sixteen has dated itself post-2017 and an answer that says fourteen is pre-2017. It is a useful check, but note what it does not do: it does not distinguish 2018 from 2022. It is necessary, not sufficient. The five provisions above are what date an answer to this sitting, and Standard A4.3.5(a) is the sharpest of them.

ul: Writing limb (b) as a second description of Title 5. The examiner asked for challenges and limitations.

Answering on the pre-2022 text and missing social connectivity, appropriately-sized PPE, the precedence of controls over PPE, the global register of deaths, and the registered owner on the security certificate.
Importing the 2025 amendments. Adopted June 2025, not in force at this sitting.
Saying the MLC is an IMO convention. It is an ILO convention.
Treating Part B Guidelines as mandatory. Article VI - Part A Standards bind; Part B must be given due consideration.
Giving only one of the two hours regimes. A Member fixes either maximum work or minimum rest, and you should give both sets of figures.
Confusing DMLC Part I (competent authority, national requirements) with Part II (shipowner, measures for ongoing compliance).
Forgetting Regulation 5.3, labour-supplying responsibilities - which is the limb that matters most to an Indian candidate.
Quoting a ratification count. Any figure you have read is almost certainly later than this sitting. Leave it out.
The five named areas in limb (a). They are a checklist. Tick every one.

Accommodation applies by build date. Standard A3.1 construction requirements bite only on ships built on or after entry into force for that Member - a point candidates almost never make and which distinguishes a read answer from a remembered one. Note that paragraph 17 on social connectivity is not a construction standard and is not limited that way.
"Less than twelve months". Standard A2.5.2(b) says less than, not "up to". The eleven-month contract exists for this reason.
"Appropriately-sized" PPE. One word, and it is the whole point of the amendment.
Prima facie evidence. The certificate is not conclusive. Naming the four triggers at Standard A5.2.1.1 is what earns the port State marks.
No more favourable treatment (Article V.7) - the MLC has its own version, and it is what stops a non-ratifying flag being a commercial advantage.
Three of nine branches of social security. An exact number in the weakest Title.
"Which is the latest set of MLC amendments in force?" - the 2022 amendments, in force 23 December 2024. The 2025 amendments are adopted but not yet in force.
"Is internet access a requirement?" - Standard A3.1 paragraph 17 requires recreational facilities including social connectivity, and the guidance addresses internet access at reasonable charges.

"What does the Convention say about PPE?" - Standard A4.3.1(b) requires all necessary appropriately-sized PPE, and Guideline B4.3.1.3 with Standard A4.3.2 puts engineering and design controls and substitution ahead of it.
"What documents prove MLC compliance, and who issues each?" - the maritime labour certificate and the DMLC; Part I by the competent authority, Part II by the shipowner.
"How long is the certificate valid and what happens in between?" - not exceeding five years, with an intermediate inspection between the second and third anniversary dates.
"State the hours of rest limits." - ten hours in any 24 and 77 in any seven days; or, on the hours-of-work basis, 14 in any 24 and 72 in any seven days.
"A seafarer has been on board thirteen months. What is wrong?" - Standard A2.5.2(b) requires the maximum service period before repatriation entitlement to be less than twelve months.
"A seafarer dies on board. What must the flag State do?" - Standard A4.3.5(a): investigate and record it, and report annually to the ILO Director-General for the global register.
"When can a PSCO go beyond checking the certificate?" - the four triggers at Standard A5.2.1.1.

blocks.p: The five Titles are the spine and they run in the order a seafarer experiences them: get on board (Title 1), terms of service (Title 2), live on board (Title 3), stay well (Title 4), who checks (Title 5). Route steps 2 to 4 are Titles 1 to 4; steps 5 to 7 are Title 5 and its shortfalls.

For limb (b), hold four failure points: who inspects (delegated, and paid by the inspected), what is inspected (paper, prima facie), who records (the seafarer records their own hours), and who pays (the ship is detained, the owner is remote).

For the 2022 additions, four words in Title order: CONNECT, FIT, PRECEDE, COUNT - social connectivity (3.1), appropriately-sized PPE (4.3), controls precede PPE (B4.3.1), deaths counted in a global register (4.3.5). The fifth, the registered owner on the security certificate, hangs off the financial security material at 4.2.

ul: Articles IV, V.7, VI - rights; no more favourable treatment; Parts A and B and substantial equivalence.
Std A1.1 minimum age 16, night work under 18. Std A1.2.7 medical certificate two years, one year under 18, colour vision six years.
Std A2.1 the employment agreement. Std A2.3.5 14/72 or 10/77. Std A2.5.1-2 repatriation and less than twelve months. Reg 2.2, 2.4, 2.7 wages, leave, manning.
Reg 3.1 accommodation, by build date. Std A3.1 para 17 recreational facilities including SOCIAL CONNECTIVITY. Reg 3.2 food and catering, free of charge.

Reg 4.1 medical care. Reg 4.2 and Appendix A4-I(g) shipowners' liability, financial security, and the REGISTERED OWNER where different. Std A4.3.1(b) appropriately-sized PPE. Std A4.3.2 with Guideline B4.3.1.3 engineering and design control and substitution PRECEDE PPE. Std A4.3.2 safety committee at five seafarers. Std A4.3.5(a) deaths investigated, recorded and reported annually to the ILO for a GLOBAL REGISTER. Reg 4.4 shore welfare. Std A4.5.2 three of nine branches.
Std A5.1.3 certificate, five years, intermediate inspection. Appendix A5-I sixteen certified areas. Reg 5.1.4, 5.1.5, 5.1.6 inspection, complaints, casualties.
Std A5.2.1.1 four PSC triggers. Appendix A5-III sixteen detailed-inspection areas. Reg 5.2.2 onshore complaints. Reg 5.3 labour-supplying responsibilities.

blocks.p: The answer was written from the ILO consolidated text including the Amendments of 2022, which is the edition operative at this sitting, and each of the five 2022 additions was located verbatim in that text and cited to its own Standard, Guideline or Appendix rather than to "the 2022 amendments" as a block.

The entry-into-force date of 23 December 2024 is taken from the corpus temporal record - itself verified against the ILO Compendium of maritime labour instruments, 4th revised edition - and from the ILO's own published notice, rather than from the consolidated text, which records the Conference session at which amendments were approved rather than the date they took effect. Two independent sources agree. The date matters because it places the amendments comfortably before this sitting.

The 2025 amendments were checked and deliberately excluded. The corpus holds them segregated from the in-force consolidation, so the exclusion was tested by probing the operative text rather than argued from memory. Their expected 2027 effective date is a projection and nothing in the Model Answer rests on it.

The number of ratifying States is not asserted anywhere. The figures available in the corpus are as at 2026 and post-date this sitting, so quoting them would be a currency error in the opposite direction. The COVID-19 crew change crisis is described qualitatively; no figure for seafarers affected is given, because no primary source for one was consulted.

classes: convention amendment in force between the sittings
later amendment adopted but not in force
notes: Intake said STABLE / LOW. That is WRONG and the error is material. Confirmed CORRECTED / HIGH from primary text.

The MLC 2022 amendments, approved at the 110th Session of the International Labour Conference on 6 June 2022, ENTERED INTO FORCE ON 23 DECEMBER 2024 - ten months before this sitting. The operative consolidation here is the Convention as amended in 2014, 2016, 2018 AND 2022. The donor was correctly written on the pre-2022 text for March 2024.

Entry into force is corroborated twice and independently: the corpus instrument log verified against the ILO Compendium of maritime labour instruments (4th revised edition, 2026), and the ILO's own published notice.

FIVE 2022 provisions were located VERBATIM in the consolidated text and INTEGRATED into the limb-(a) sections where they belong, not appended as an amendment paragraph: Standard A3.1 paragraph 17 (social connectivity, with guidance on internet access) into the Title 3 accommodation section; Standard A4.3 paragraph 1(b) (appropriately-sized PPE) and Guideline B4.3.1 paragraph 3 with Standard A4.3 paragraph 2 (engineering and design control and substitution take precedence over PPE) into the Title 4 health and safety section; Standard A4.3 paragraph 5(a) (deaths investigated, recorded and reported annually to the ILO Director-General for a global register) into the same section as a flag-State duty; and Appendix A4-I(g) (registered owner named where different from the shipowner) into the financial security material.

EVERY donor statement describing the 2022 amendments as not yet in force has been found and reversed. This was the single largest re-anchoring job on the paper. The donor's Study Guide section headed 'what that excludes from a March 2024 answer' has been replaced by a section stating what the 2022 set REQUIRES.

FUTURE-DATE CONTROL, and it is armed. The 2025 amendments were ADOPTED at the 113th Session in June 2025 - FOUR MONTHS BEFORE this sitting - but are NOT in force, with an expected effective date in 2027. They are quarantined and appear nowhere in the Model Answer. They are mentioned in the Study Guide only, expressly labelled as a later development. Adoption is not entry into force - the same lesson as the IMO Net-Zero Framework in February 2026 and the Merchant Shipping Act 2025 in QP2607.
The corpus deliberately holds the two consolidations separately, so the exclusion was tested by term-probing the in-force text rather than argued from recollection.

RATIFICATION COUNT DELIBERATELY OMITTED. The figures available in the corpus (110 Members, over 96 per cent of world gross tonnage) are as at 2026 and post-date this sitting. Quoting them would be future-date contamination, so no count is asserted anywhere.
Appendix A5-I still carries SIXTEEN items and remains a valid dating marker, but it does not distinguish 2018 from 2022 and is recorded as necessary but not sufficient.

Limb (b) reuses UNCHANGED except for one added proposition: the global register at Standard A4.3.5(a) is a partial answer to the enforcement-data gap the donor criticises, and the registered-owner requirement attacks the layered-ownership complaint. Both were integrated rather than bolted on.

questions.understand_first: The MLC is an ILO convention, not an IMO one, and that shapes everything about it. It regulates the EMPLOYMENT RELATIONSHIP rather than the ship, which is why its enforcement machinery had to be borrowed from the IMO world - certification, port State control, no more favourable treatment - and bolted onto a labour instrument. Limb (a) is a coverage test across the five Titles; limb (b) asks you to explain why an instrument with that much machinery still leaves seafarers abandoned, overworked and unpaid. The honest answer to limb (b) is that the enforcement is documentary, the inspector is often paid by the inspected, and the seafarer writes their own hours record. TWO DATE WARNINGS DECIDE THIS ANSWER, and they run in opposite directions. The 2022 amendments ARE in force - they took effect on 23 December 2024, ten months before this paper - so social connectivity, appropriately-sized PPE, the precedence of engineering controls over PPE, the global register of seafarer deaths and the naming of the registered owner are all simply the law. But the 2025 amendments, adopted four months before this sitting, are NOT in force and must be kept out. Adoption is not entry into force.
questions.memory_cue: The five Titles run in the order a seafarer meets them: GET ON BOARD, TERMS, LIVE, WELL, CHECK (2, 3, 4, 5). Then limb (b) has four failure points to attack in route step 7: INSPECT, PAPER, RECORD, PAY (7). For the 2022 additions, four words in Title order: CONNECT, FIT, PRECEDE, COUNT (4).

quick_revision.recall_15s: ILO convention adopted at the 94th (Maritime) Session, 2006 - the fourth pillar. Articles, Regulations and Code; Part A Standards mandatory, Part B Guidelines given due consideration; Article VI.3 substantial equivalence. Five Titles: minimum requirements; conditions of employment; accommodation and catering; health, welfare and social security; compliance and enforcement. Age 16; night work under 18 banned; medical certificate two years, one under 18. Hours: 14 in 24 and 72 in 7, or rest 10 in 24 and 77 in 7. Repatriation after service periods that must be LESS THAN twelve months. Std A3.1 para 17 - recreational facilities INCLUDING social connectivity. Std A4.3.1(b) - appropriately-sized PPE; B4.3.1.3 - engineering and design controls PRECEDE PPE; Std A4.3.5(a) - deaths reported annually to the ILO for a GLOBAL REGISTER. Appendix A4-I(g) - registered owner named where different. Certificate not exceeding five years plus an intermediate inspection; DMLC Part I authority, Part II shipowner; Appendix A5-I sixteen areas. PSC accepts the certificate as prima facie evidence, with four triggers for detailed inspection. At THIS sitting the amendments in force are 2014, 2016, 2018 and 2022 - the 2025 amendments are adopted but NOT in force.
