quick_revision.critical_regulation: Standard A2.3.5 - a Member fixes either maximum hours of work, not exceeding 14 in any 24-hour period and 72 in any seven-day period, or minimum hours of rest, not less than ten in any 24-hour period and 77 in any seven-day period. Read it with Standard A5.1.3 on the maritime labour certificate and Standard A5.2.1.1 on the four triggers for a detailed port State inspection.
quick_revision.major_trap: Answering on the PRE-2022 text. The MLC 2022 amendments entered into force on 23 December 2024, ten months before this sitting, and are simply the law here - social connectivity as a recreational facility (Standard A3.1 paragraph 17), appropriately-sized personal protective equipment (Standard A4.3.1(b)), the precedence of engineering and design control and substitution over PPE (Guideline B4.3.1.3 with Standard A4.3.2), the investigation, recording and annual reporting of seafarer deaths to the ILO Director-General for a global register (Standard A4.3.5(a)), and the naming of the registered owner on the financial security certificate (Appendix A4-I(g)). Four of the five fall in Title 3 and Title 4, which the examiner has expressly named. THE OPPOSITE TRAP IS ALSO LIVE: the 2025 amendments were ADOPTED at the 113th Session in June 2025, four months before this sitting, but are NOT in force - expected 2027 - so any material describing them in the present tense is describing a later state of the law. Adoption is not entry into force.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the MLC question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What the Convention is and how it is built. 2 (a) Minimum requirements and the employment agreement. 3 (a) Hours, wages, leave, repatriation, manning. 4 (a) Accommodation, catering, health, welfare, social security. 5 (b) Flag State certification and inspection. 6 (b) Port State control and the labour-supplying State. 7 (b) Challenges and limitations.
retrieval_cards.why: Steps 2-4 are the five areas the examiner named; step 7 is where limb (b) scores.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which set of MLC amendments is the latest IN FORCE at this sitting, and which set must be kept out?
retrieval_cards.answer: The 2022 amendments, approved at the 110th Session in June 2022, entered into force on 23 December 2024 and are in force here. The 2025 amendments, adopted at the 113th Session in June 2025 - four months before this sitting - are NOT in force, and are expected to take effect in 2027. Adoption is not entry into force.
retrieval_cards.why: Both traps are live: an old answer misses the 2022 set, a current source imports the 2025 set.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What do the 2022 amendments require that an older answer would miss?
retrieval_cards.answer: Social connectivity as part of recreational facilities (Standard A3.1 paragraph 17, with guidance on internet access at reasonable charges); all necessary appropriately-sized personal protective equipment (Standard A4.3.1(b)); engineering and design control and substitution taking precedence over PPE (Guideline B4.3.1.3 with Standard A4.3.2); investigation, recording and annual reporting of seafarer deaths to the ILO Director-General for a global register (Standard A4.3.5(a)); and naming the registered owner on the financial security certificate where different from the shipowner (Appendix A4-I(g)).
retrieval_cards.why: Four of the five sit in Title 3 and Title 4, which limb (a) expressly names.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the MLC now say about personal protective equipment?
retrieval_cards.answer: Standard A4.3.1(b) requires reasonable precautions including the provision of all necessary APPROPRIATELY-SIZED personal protective equipment. Guideline B4.3.1 paragraph 3, read with Standard A4.3 paragraph 2, requires engineering and design control and the substitution of the dangerous by the less dangerous to have PRECEDENCE over PPE.
retrieval_cards.why: The hierarchy of controls is now express in the Convention - a design and management duty, not a stores duty.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between Part A and Part B of the MLC Code?
retrieval_cards.answer: Article VI - Part A contains Standards and is mandatory. Part B contains Guidelines which are not mandatory, but Members must give them due consideration. Article VI.3 also permits substantial equivalence, allowing a Member to implement a Part A Standard differently provided it is substantially equivalent in achieving the general object and purpose.
retrieval_cards.why: Treating Part B as binding is the most common structural error on this topic.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the MLC hours of work and hours of rest limits.
retrieval_cards.answer: Standard A2.3.5 - a Member fixes either maximum hours of work, not exceeding 14 in any 24-hour period and 72 in any seven-day period; or minimum hours of rest, not less than ten in any 24-hour period and 77 in any seven-day period. Rest may be in no more than two periods, one of at least six hours, with no more than fourteen hours between them.
retrieval_cards.why: Both regimes are needed - the Convention offers an either/or, not a single rule.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How long is the maritime labour certificate valid, and what accompanies it?
retrieval_cards.answer: Standard A5.1.3.1 - a period not exceeding five years, with an intermediate inspection between the second and third anniversary dates under A5.1.3.2. It is accompanied by the Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance: Part I by the competent authority listing the national requirements, Part II by the shipowner setting out the measures for ongoing compliance between inspections.
retrieval_cards.why: The Part I / Part II split is asked in almost every oral on this topic.

retrieval_cards.prompt: When may a port State officer go beyond checking the certificate?
retrieval_cards.answer: Standard A5.2.1.1 - where the required documents are not produced, not maintained, falsely maintained, lack required information or are otherwise invalid; where there are clear grounds for believing conditions do not conform; where there are reasonable grounds to believe the ship changed flag to avoid compliance; or where there is a complaint. Appendix A5-III lists the sixteen areas open to detailed inspection.
retrieval_cards.why: The certificate is prima facie evidence only, and these four triggers rebut it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A seafarer dies on board. What does the Convention require of the flag State?
retrieval_cards.answer: Standard A4.3.5(a) - the Member must ensure that all deaths of seafarers employed, engaged or working on board ships that fly its flag are adequately investigated and recorded, and reported on an annual basis to the Director-General of the International Labour Office to be published in a global register.
retrieval_cards.why: New with the 2022 amendments, and usable twice - as a limb (a) duty and as a limb (b) partial answer to the data gap.

retrieval_cards.prompt: In what circumstances is a seafarer entitled to repatriation, and after how long?
retrieval_cards.answer: Standard A2.5.1 - when the employment agreement expires while abroad; when it is terminated by the shipowner or by the seafarer for justified reasons; and when the seafarer is no longer able to carry out the duties or cannot be expected to. Standard A2.5.2(b) requires the maximum service period on board after which repatriation falls due to be less than twelve months.
retrieval_cards.why: "Less than twelve months" - not "up to" - is why eleven-month contracts exist.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why are hours-of-rest records the most commonly falsified MLC requirement?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the record is generated by the person whose hours it records, on a ship manned to the minimum safe manning document, under commercial pressure. Port turnarounds, inspections and drills are absorbed by the crew and never reach the record. The structural conflict, not individual dishonesty, is the point.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the strongest single answer available for limb (b).

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does Article V.7 provide and why does it matter commercially?
retrieval_cards.answer: Each Member must implement its responsibilities so that ships flying the flag of a State which has not ratified the Convention do not receive more favourable treatment than those of a ratifying State. It removes the commercial advantage of flagging out to a non-party.
retrieval_cards.why: The MLC has its own no-more-favourable-treatment clause, distinct from the IMO ones.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What responsibilities does Regulation 5.3 place on a labour-supplying State?
retrieval_cards.answer: Responsibilities for the recruitment, placement and social protection of its seafarers - implemented through Regulation 1.4 on recruitment and placement services and Regulation 4.5 on social security. It is the limb that applies to India as a major supplier of seafarers rather than as a flag State.
retrieval_cards.why: Routinely omitted, and the most directly relevant limb for an Indian candidate.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does Appendix A5-I list sixteen items, and what does that NOT tell you?
retrieval_cards.answer: The 2014 amendments added financial security for repatriation and financial security relating to shipowners' liability to the fourteen original items. It dates an answer to post-2017, but it does NOT distinguish the 2018 state from the 2022 state - the sixteen is unchanged by the 2022 amendments.
retrieval_cards.why: A useful dating marker, but necessary rather than sufficient at this sitting.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two limbs of eight marks with very different demands. Limb (a) is a coverage test across five named areas - employment contracts, working hours, accommodation, health and safety, medical care and welfare. Limb (b) is evaluative and names three targets - flag State jurisdiction, port State control and shipowner non-compliance - so describing Title 5 is not an answer to it.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16 marks printed as 8 + 8, identical to the March 2024 sitting. Limb (a) is best spent across the Titles in order so that none of the five named areas is dropped; limb (b) needs the machinery described briefly and the criticism at length.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate can name Standards, not just describe conditions - A2.3.5 for hours, A5.1.3 for the certificate, A5.2.1.1 for the PSC triggers - and can then say why an instrument with that machinery still fails seafarers in practice. At this sitting the discriminator is whether the candidate is current with the 2022 amendments, four of whose five additions fall in the Titles the examiner has named.
primary_source_plan: Establish FIRST which amendment set was in force at the sitting, before drafting anything
Obtain the ILO consolidation that matches that state - the text including the 2022 amendments
Locate every 2022 addition VERBATIM and cite it to its own Standard, Guideline or Appendix
Establish the entry-into-force date from a source independent of the consolidated text
Check whether any LATER amendment set has been adopted but not yet entered into force, and quarantine it
Take every number from the operative text: hours, certificate validity, A5-I count
Do not assert ratification counts or crew-change figures without a source dated at or before the sitting
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: HIGH - and it materialised in BOTH directions. The 2022 amendments entered into force between the donor sitting and this one, so the same question has a materially different answer at the two sittings. Separately the 2025 amendments were adopted four months before this sitting but are not in force, so current material describes a state of the law that had not yet arrived.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW for the Convention itself. India is a Party and the Convention applies uniformly. Regulation 5.3 on labour-supplying responsibilities is the limb of most direct relevance to an Indian candidate and is included for that reason.
technical_ambiguities: Which amendment sets were operative at the sitting date, and which were merely adopted
Whether Part B Guidelines are binding - they are not, which matters because the hierarchy of controls sits partly in Guideline B4.3.1
Whether the maximum service period before repatriation is twelve months or less than twelve
Whether Appendix A5-I has fourteen or sixteen items, and whether the 2022 amendments changed the count
Whether the maritime labour certificate is conclusive or prima facie evidence
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Structure and amendment state first, because the amendment state decides what the rest of the answer may say; then the Titles in order for limb (a), with the 2022 additions threaded into the sections they amend rather than gathered into a block; then the enforcement machinery compactly; then the criticism, organised around who inspects, what is inspected, who records and who pays.
decomposition_gate.note: Command verbs -> command_verbs. Required answer components -> decomposition. Internal reuse map -> reuse_evidence. Not duplicated here.

reverify_before_publication.claim: At the October 2025 sitting the MLC is in force as amended in 2014, 2016, 2018 and 2022, and the 2022 amendments took effect on 23 December 2024
reverify_before_publication.why: The single load-bearing temporal claim on this question, and the one that makes the answer different from the same question at the March 2024 sitting. Corroborated from two independent sources - the corpus instrument log verified against the ILO Compendium, and the ILO's own published notice. Re-confirm before publication against ILO treaty status information.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The 2025 amendments were adopted at the 113th Session in June 2025 but were NOT in force at this sitting
reverify_before_publication.why: A negative claim about the state of the law at a date now in the past, and the exact kind of thing a later editor working from current ILO pages will 'correct'. The corpus holds the 2025 set segregated so the exclusion can be re-tested by probing the in-force consolidation. Flagged so that the quarantine is not quietly lifted.

reverify_before_publication.claim: Each of the five 2022 additions is cited to its own Standard, Guideline or Appendix - A3.1 para 17, A4.3 para 1(b), B4.3.1 para 3, A4.3 para 5(a) and Appendix A4-I(g)
reverify_before_publication.why: Each was located verbatim in the consolidated text. Paragraph numbering within a consolidated ILO text is the most likely thing to be mis-transcribed, so re-check the paragraph numbers against the consolidation before publication.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The COVID-19 crew change crisis as an illustration of enforcement limits
reverify_before_publication.why: Described qualitatively and without figures. No primary source was consulted for the scale of the crisis, and none is cited. If a figure is ever added it must be sourced.

reverify_before_publication.claim: Recognized organizations are paid by the shipowners they inspect, and this is a structural conflict
reverify_before_publication.why: A statement of how the commercial relationship works, not of a rule. Regulation 5.1.2 authorises delegation but says nothing about who pays. Offered as evaluation in limb (b), which is what the limb asks for, and flagged as judgement rather than citation.
